Key Content — Year 12 Level

Core Knowledge

Essential content for VCE Revolutions Unit 4 AoS 2. Select a topic.

Declaration of the Rights of Man and Citizen (1789)

Adopted by the National Assembly on 26 August 1789, the Declaration of the Rights of Man and Citizen is the Revolution's founding ideological statement and its most enduring legacy. Drafted by Lafayette (influenced by the American Declaration of Independence) and revised by the Assembly, its 17 articles proclaimed that "the principle of all sovereignty resides essentially in the nation" and that "the aim of all political association is the preservation of the natural and imprescriptible rights of man: liberty, property, security, and resistance to oppression."

The Declaration was genuinely revolutionary in several respects: it abolished the legal distinction between estates, proclaimed equality before the law, established freedom of speech and of the press, and enshrined the principle of popular sovereignty. But it was also conspicuously silent on women (Olympe de Gouges's Declaration of the Rights of Woman, 1791, was its direct challenge) and did nothing to extend rights to enslaved people in the colonies (the Haitian Revolution of 1791 was the enslaved response).

Schama: the Declaration was "the birth certificate of modernity" — but its universalist language masked profound exclusions that would define the Revolution's limits.

Constitutional Experiments 1791–1795

The Revolution produced three constitutions in four years — each reflecting a different balance of power. The Constitution of 1791 established a constitutional monarchy: Louis XVI retained executive power but was subject to the Legislative Assembly; voting was restricted to "active citizens" (those paying taxes equivalent to three days' labour). It was almost immediately superseded by events — Louis's flight to Varennes (June 1791) destroyed whatever remained of monarchist credibility.

The Constitution of 1793 (Year I) — the most democratic France had ever produced — guaranteed universal male suffrage, the right to work and education, and the right of popular insurrection against oppressive government. It was suspended before it could be implemented, as the Committee of Public Safety assumed emergency powers. The Constitution of Year III (1795) was a conservative reaction to the Terror: it restored property qualifications for voting, created a bicameral legislature (Council of Five Hundred and Council of Ancients), and established the five-man Directory as executive.

Declaration of Rights of Man Constitution of 1791 Constitution of 1793 Constitution of Year III

War and Foreign Invasion

War with Austria and Prussia (declared April 1792) transformed the Revolution's character. Initially disastrous — the French army was poorly led, poorly supplied, and undermined by the emigration of thousands of noble officers — the war rapidly became an existential crisis. The Prussian Duke of Brunswick's manifesto (July 1792), threatening to destroy Paris if the royal family was harmed, radicalised Parisian opinion and precipitated the insurrection of 10 August that overthrew the monarchy.

The unexpected French victory at Valmy (20 September 1792) — the day the Convention abolished the monarchy and declared the republic — transformed the war's strategic and ideological stakes. France was no longer defending itself; it was spreading revolution. By 1793 France was at war with Austria, Prussia, Britain, the Dutch Republic, Spain and Sardinia simultaneously — the First Coalition. This external military pressure directly caused the radicalisation of the Revolution: the emergency powers of the Committee of Public Safety, the Terror, the levée en masse — all were responses to the existential threat of foreign invasion.

Doyle: "The war was the matrix within which the Terror developed. Without the military crisis of 1793, the radical measures of the Year II are inconceivable."

Counter-Revolution: the Vendée

The Vendée uprising (March 1793) was the Revolution's most traumatic internal crisis. When the National Convention decreed the levée en masse — conscripting 300,000 men — the Catholic and royalist peasants of the western département of Vendée rose in armed rebellion. They rejected conscription, the Civil Constitution of the Clergy (which had subordinated the Church to the state), and the Revolution's assault on their traditional way of life.

The ensuing civil war was extraordinarily brutal. Republican forces — the "colonnes infernales" (infernal columns) — systematically destroyed villages, massacred civilians, and drowned prisoners in the Loire in mass executions known as noyades. Estimates of deaths range from 200,000 to 250,000 — making the Vendée one of the bloodiest episodes in revolutionary history. Whether it constituted genocide remains one of the most contested questions in French historiography. For the Revolution, the Vendée demonstrated that the new regime's enemies were not only foreign monarchs but also significant portions of its own population who rejected its values.

War of the First Coalition Battle of Valmy Vendée Uprising Levée en Masse Colonnes Infernales

The Committee of Public Safety and the Terror

The Terror (September 1793 – July 1794) was the Revolution's most controversial consequence — simultaneously its most radical phase and its greatest betrayal of its own ideals. The Committee of Public Safety, dominated by Maximilien Robespierre from July 1793, assumed de facto dictatorial power over France. The Law of Suspects (September 1793) empowered authorities to arrest anyone suspected of counter-revolutionary sympathies. The Revolutionary Tribunal — established in March 1793 — was redesigned in June 1794 (Law of 22 Prairial) to deny accused persons the right to legal counsel or to call witnesses, making conviction and execution the overwhelming norm.

The statistics of the Terror: approximately 40,000 people were executed (16,594 officially, the remainder by summary execution or dying in prison); 300,000 were imprisoned. The guillotine — the Revolution's great leveller, which killed noble and commoner alike — became the Terror's defining symbol. Its victims included Queen Marie Antoinette (October 1793), the Girondins (October 1793), the radical Hébertists (March 1794), and the moderate Dantonists (April 1794) — Robespierre turned on every faction in turn until his own execution in Thermidor.

Robespierre and the Republic of Virtue

Robespierre's justification for the Terror was ideological as well as practical: France was fighting a war for its survival, and enemies within were as dangerous as enemies without. More profoundly, he articulated the Terror as the instrument of a "Republic of Virtue" — a political community of civic equality and republican morality that could only be achieved by eliminating those who corrupted it. His concept of virtue drew directly on Rousseau's general will: the revolutionary government expressed the will of the sovereign people, and those who opposed it were not merely political enemies but traitors to humanity itself.

The Terror's historiographical debate remains fierce. Soboul sees it as a necessary response to the military emergency of 1793–94, driven by genuine popular pressure from the sans-culottes. Schama sees it as inherent in the Revolution's violent logic from the start — the Terror was not an aberration but a culmination. Furet argues the Terror's logic was embedded in the revolutionary ideology of popular sovereignty itself: once "the people" became the source of all authority, anyone who opposed the revolution could be cast as an enemy of the people and liquidated.

Committee of Public Safety Law of Suspects Revolutionary Tribunal Republic of Virtue Law of 22 Prairial

Social and Economic Consequences

The Revolution's social consequences were profound and uneven. The abolition of feudalism (4 August 1789) and the nationalisation of Church property — sold as biens nationaux (national goods) — redistributed approximately 10% of French land. The primary beneficiaries were the bourgeoisie and wealthy peasants who had capital to purchase confiscated lands; the rural poor rarely benefited. The metric system, standardised weights and measures, and a new revolutionary calendar (Year I beginning September 1792) were deliberate attempts to rationalise French society along Enlightenment lines.

Economic conditions deteriorated sharply during the Terror. The assignat — paper currency backed by confiscated Church land — inflated catastrophically: by 1795 it had lost 96% of its face value. Food shortages, price controls (the General Maximum, September 1793), and wartime requisitioning created acute suffering for urban workers. The General Maximum attempted to fix prices of bread and other essentials; it was abandoned after Thermidor, triggering price explosions that devastated the sans-culottes who had been the Terror's primary political base.

Dechristianisation and Cultural Revolution

The dechristianisation campaign of 1793–94 was one of the Revolution's most radical and divisive initiatives. Churches were converted to "Temples of Reason"; religious services were banned; priests were pressured to resign or marry; the Christian calendar was replaced by the revolutionary calendar. The campaign was driven partly by Hébertist radicals, partly by genuine anti-clericalism, and partly by the practical need to strip Church wealth and property for the war effort.

Robespierre himself opposed atheistic dechristianisation, replacing it with the Cult of the Supreme Being — a deist civic religion that attempted to harness religious sentiment for the Revolution without submitting to either Christianity or atheism. His Festival of the Supreme Being (8 June 1794) was simultaneously his greatest triumph of political theatre and, many historians argue, the beginning of his political downfall — his rivals feared he was setting himself up as a new religious authority.

Biens Nationaux Assignat General Maximum Dechristianisation Cult of Supreme Being

The Thermidorian Reaction (1794)

Robespierre's fall came suddenly on 9 Thermidor Year II (27 July 1794). A coalition of Montagnards who feared they were next on his list, Thermidorian moderates, and former terrorists united against him. Arrested in the Convention, Robespierre attempted suicide; he was guillotined the following day along with Saint-Just and Couthon — the architects of the Terror's final phase. The fall of Robespierre did not immediately end the Terror, but it ended its political justification.

The Thermidorian Reaction was the Revolution's conservative turn. The Committee of Public Safety was reorganised and stripped of its emergency powers; the Revolutionary Tribunal was reformed; political prisoners were released; the Law of Suspects was repealed. The former terrorists — the "Thermidorians" — sought to consolidate the Revolution's gains (constitutional government, legal equality, property rights) without the Terror's excesses. But Thermidor was not a restoration: Louis XVII remained in prison (he died in June 1795), and the Republic continued.

The Directory (1795) and Revolutionary Legacy

The Constitution of Year III (1795) established the Directory — a five-man executive body — alongside a bicameral legislature. It was a deliberately anti-democratic constitution: property qualifications for voting were restored; the Constitution of 1793 (with its universal suffrage) was discarded. The Directory was chronically unstable, surviving by manipulating election results and relying on military force. Its inability to resolve France's financial crisis or end the foreign wars created the conditions for Napoleon's coup of 18 Brumaire (November 1799).

The revolutionary legacy of 1789–1795 was paradoxical and vast. The Declaration of the Rights of Man inspired constitutions across Europe and the Americas. The abolition of feudalism permanently transformed French social structure. The metric system, the concept of popular sovereignty, and the idea of the nation in arms were global exports of the Revolution. But the Terror demonstrated that revolutionary idealism could generate systematic state violence on an unprecedented scale — a lesson the 20th century would rediscover at far greater cost.

Thermidorian Reaction 9 Thermidor Directory Constitution of Year III Revolutionary Legacy

Key historians for Unit 4 AoS 2 — the consequences of the French Revolution.

Albert Soboul

1914–1982 | Marxist / Social

The sans-culottes were the Revolution's driving popular force. The Terror was a necessary emergency response to the military crisis of 1793–94, driven by genuine popular pressure from below. The Revolution was a bourgeois revolution that unleashed — but ultimately failed to satisfy — working-class aspirations. Essential for questions about popular movements and the Terror's causes.

Simon Schama

b. 1945 | Revisionist / Cultural

Citizens (1989): The Terror was not an aberration but inherent in the Revolution's violent logic from the beginning. The Revolution unleashed forces it could not control. Violence was not imposed on the Revolution from outside (by war or counter-revolution) but was central to its identity. One of the most powerful challenges to the Marxist tradition.

William Doyle

b. 1942 | Revisionist / Political

The Terror was generated primarily by the war emergency of 1793 — without foreign invasion and the Vendée, the radical measures of the Year II are inconceivable. Doyle's revisionism challenges both the Marxist (Terror as class war) and Schama's culturalist (Terror as inherent) interpretations. Essential for balanced evaluation of the Terror's causes.

François Furet

1927–1997 | Liberal / Revisionist

The Terror's logic was embedded in the revolutionary ideology of popular sovereignty: once "the people" became the source of all authority, political opponents could be cast as enemies of the people and eliminated. Furet's "political" interpretation of the Terror — as the consequence of radical democratic ideology — is essential for AoS 2 questions about political consequences.

Peter McPhee

b. 1948 | Social / Popular

McPhee foregrounds the diversity of revolutionary experience across gender, class, region and race. The Revolution's consequences were profoundly unequal — genuinely transformative for the bourgeoisie and male peasant property-owners; far more ambiguous for women, the rural poor, and enslaved people in the colonies. Essential for questions about diverse social groups.

Lynn Hunt

b. 1945 | Cultural / Gender

Hunt's work on political culture, gender, and the family romance of the Revolution illuminates how new concepts of citizenship simultaneously included men as universal subjects and excluded women. The Revolution's rhetoric of fraternity (brotherhood) was inherently gendered. Essential for questions about women's experiences and the limits of revolutionary equality.

David Bell

b. 1961 | Cultural / Intellectual

Bell's work on nationalism and total war argues the Revolution invented modern nationalism and the concept of total war — mobilising an entire nation's resources for military conflict. The levée en masse (1793) was the first mass conscription in modern European history. Essential for questions about the Revolution's long-term international consequences.

    Section A — Short-answer questions with sources

    Question 1 (25 marks) · The American Revolution

    Read Sources 1–4 below, then answer parts a–e.

    Source 1

    A historical interpretation, published in 2003, of changes in the British management of the colonies.

    With the French defeated, the British government could turn its attention to tightening control over the colonies. It needed revenues1 to pay for the war and looked to the colonies for that. Also, the colonial trade had become more and more important to the British economy, and more profitable: it had amounted to about 500,000 pounds in 1700 but by 1770 was worth 2,800,000 pounds.

    So, the American leadership was less in need of English rule, the English more in need of the colonists’ wealth. The elements were there for conflict.

    Source: Howard Zinn, A People’s History of the United States (New York: HarperCollins, 2003), 60.

    1. revenues – income and profits
    Source 2

    This engraving by Paul Revere is titled ‘A View of the Year 1765’ and was first published in Boston in 1765. It depicts a dragon backed up to a ledge by individuals representing colonial interests. The dragon clutches a rolled-up copy of the Magna Charta1, while two demons fly directly above.

    Beneath the group of people are the words ‘United Provinces’. The person closest to the dragon is attempting to slay the beast with a sword. To the dragon’s left lie two bodies of individuals known to support British parliamentary supremacy.

    To the far right is a tree labelled ‘Liberty Tree August 14, 1765’, with an effigy of John Huske (a member of British Parliament) hanged from its branches. In front are two men conversing and pointing to the effigy. One states, ‘there’s that villain H-k’, and the other, ‘I see he’s got a high place’.

    1. Magna Charta – this refers to the Magna Carta (latin for ‘Great Charter’), a document signed in 1215 guaranteeing the rights and political liberties of all people in England; it sought to prevent the king from exploiting his power
    Source 3

    An extract from a letter written by George Washington from the Winter Encampment at Valley Forge on 23 December 1777. The letter is addressed to Henry Laurens, the president of the Second Continental Congress at the time.

    To Henry Laurens
    Valley Forge Decemb. 23d 1777.
    Sir

    Full as I was in my representation of matters in the Commissary’s department1 yesterday, fresh and more powerful reasons oblige me to add, that I am now convinced beyond a doubt, that unless some great and capital change suddenly takes place in that line this Army must inevitably be reduced to one or other of these three things.

    Starve—dissolve—or disperse, in order to obtain subsistence2 in the best manner they can. [Rest] assured, Sir, this is not an exaggerated picture, and that I have abundant reason to support what I say.

    Yesterday afternoon receiving information that the Enemy, in force, had left the City, and were advancing towards Derby, with apparent design to forage and draw subsistence from that part of the Country, I ordered the Troops to be in readiness, that I might give every Opposition in my power; when behold! to my great mortification, I was not only informed, but convinced, that the Men were unable to stir on account of provision, and that a dangerous mutiny, begun the night before and which with difficulty was suppressed by the spirited exertions of some Officers, was still much to be apprehended for want of this Article.

    This brought forth the only Commissary in the purchasing line in this Camp, and with him this melancholy and alarming truth, That he had not a single hoof of any kind to slaughter, and not more than 25 Barrells of Flour! From hence form an opinion of our situation, when I add, that he could not tell when to expect any.

    All I could do under these circumstances was, to send out a few light parties to watch and harrass [sic] the Enemy, whilst other parties were instantly detached different ways to collect, if possible, as much provision as would satisfy the present pressing wants of the Soldiery—But will this answer?

    No Sir: three or four days bad weather would prove our destruction.

    What then is to become of the Army this Winter? and if we are as often without Provisions now, as with them, what is to become of us in the Spring, when our force will be collected, with the aid perhaps of Militia3, to take advantage of an early campaign before the Enemy can be reinforced?

    These are considerations of great magnitude—meriting the closest attention, and will, when my own reputation is so intimately connected and to be affected by the event, justify my saying that the present Commissaries are by no means equal to the execution of the Office, or that the disaffection of the people is past [belief].

    Source: ‘From George Washington to Henry Laurens, 23 December 1777,’ Founders Online, National Archives, <https://founders.archives.gov/documents/Washington/03-12-02-0628> [Original source: Frank E. Grizzard Jr and David R. Hoth, eds, The Papers of George Washington: Revolutionary War Series, 26 October 1777 – 25 December 1777, vol. 12 (Charlottesville: University Press of Virginia, 2002), 683–687.]

    1. Commissary’s department – a military department with financial and administrative control that authorises the purchase and delivery of supplies
    2. subsistence – the action or means of supporting oneself
    3. militia – citizens to be called up for military service in support of the regular Continental soldiers
    Source 4

    A historical interpretation, published in 1992, of James Madison and his role in drafting the Constitution of the United States.

    Historians ordinarily tell two kinds of stories about the origins of the Bill of Rights. The first story retraces the rough path that the Federalists followed from their initial refusal to accept any amendments to the proposed Constitution, to their recognition of the political capital1 that Antifederalists were gaining through their repeated calls for a Bill of Rights, and so to James Madison’s decision to make the speedy adoption of suitable amendments an urgent priority of the First Federal Congress. In the standard interpretation, the Bill of Rights was largely a product of the expedient2, even cynical political maneuvers3 of both Federalists and Antifederalists, rather than an expression of truly libertarian concerns.

    Though Madison receives well deserved credit for his heroic labors in pushing the amendments through an indifferent Congress, historians still debate whether even his actions were more … of a campaign conversion prompted by a tough electoral race, … or, alternatively, of a principled reassessment of the value that bills of rights could play in preserving the liberties of republican citizens.

    Source: Jack N. Rakove, ‘James Madison and the Bill of Rights: A Broader Context,’ Presidential Studies Quarterly 22, no. 4 (1992): 667.

    1. political capital – an individual’s ability to influence political decisions
    2. expedient – convenient and to one’s advantage
    3. maneuvers – (manoeuvre) to carefully manipulate someone or something to achieve an end

    Suggested discussion points/sample response
