    B3 MARKSOUTLINE↩ Restored
    Outline how Source 2 depicts the colonial response to the Stamp Act of 1765.
    0 words · aim for ~50
    HTAV 2025/2026 Guide to Responses — suggested discussion points and sample material, not the only acceptable answer.
    • The verb ‘outline’ indicates that students should give a high-level overview or summary of the main ideas. This will work best with concise, full sentences.
    • There is no requirement for students to use their own knowledge. It is possible to achieve full marks using the source alone. However, some students may choose to draw on their own knowledge to contextualise or expand on ideas in the source.
    • As the question is worth 3 marks, it would be appropriate for students to discuss any three features of the image.
    Suggested discussion points
    • Colonists argued that by introducing policies such as the Stamp Act without the people’s consent, British authorities violated the rights and liberties of their English subjects, as symbolised by the ‘Magna Charta’ (Magna Carta).
    • Source 2 suggests that the colonists’ response was a collective and united one. This is shown by the ‘United Provinces’, who are depicted in a defensive stance with weapons raised against England (the dragon). Students may also mention the liberty pole and cap held by one of the colonies (V = Virginia).
    • The hanging effigy of John Huske (a member of British Parliament and perceived supporter of the Stamp Act at the time) shows that the colonists used intimidation and the threat of violence against British officials in response to the Stamp Act. (‘August 14’ refers to the date that the effigy of Andrew Oliver [stamp distributor for Massachusetts] was hanged and burnt, and his house attacked.)
    C9 MARKSEVALUATE↩ Restored
    Evaluate the significance of the actions of the Committees of Correspondence as a cause of the American Revolution. Use evidence to support your response.
    0 words · aim for ~220
    HTAV 2025/2026 Guide to Responses — suggested discussion points and sample material, not the only acceptable answer.
    Suggested discussion points
    • The command term for this question is ‘evaluate’. This means that students should aim to form a judgement.
    • The question asks students to explore the significance of the actions of the Committees of Correspondence. That is, rather than simply describing what the actions were, students should form arguments about why they can be considered important in bringing about a revolution.
    • Strong responses will meaningfully explore the extent to which the actions of the Committees of Correspondence caused the revolution. However, it may be appropriate to argue that these were not the most significant causes of the revolution and to develop a counterargument that other causes, such as the actions of other groups and movements, may be more significant.
    Actions of the Committees of Correspondence
    • The first Committees of Correspondence were formed in Boston and New York in response to the Stamp Act (1765).
    • They were groups involved in ideological discourse and political analysis throughout various stages of the revolution. They evolved from colony-based movements from 1772 into a form of shadow government by 1774.
      • 1770: After the Boston Massacre (March 1770), committees began to form to communicate, unite and advance the case for revolution.
      • 1772: Samuel Adams formalised the Boston Committee of Correspondence in response to the government’s decision to use Crown funds to pay the governor’s and court judges’ salaries, making them dependant on the Crown rather than the people in assembly.
      • 1773: The Virginia House of Burgesses established the Virginia Committee of Correspondence, the first colony-level committee. Thomas Jefferson and Patrick Henry were members.
      • 1773: The Committees had a combined total of about 7000–8000 members.
      • 1774: The Committees shifted their focus towards taking action and formulated a plan of resistance to the Coercive Acts. The Committees jointly organised the First Continental Congress (5 September–26 October), where 56 representatives from 12 of the 13 colonies convened in response to the Coercive Acts.
    • The Committees of Correspondence were responsible for:
      • communicating their aim of creating unity among the colonies
      • working collaboratively for letter writing campaigns
      • providing updates on British troop movements
      • mobilising resistance to the British by organising supplies, men and economic support from merchants for acts of rebellion.
    • The Committees’ actions were significant in terms of how they consolidated their ideas and worked to challenge the existing order.
    • The Committees were also influential because they connected important people.
    • They established a model of political government that birthed iconic leaders and stimulated intellectual debates. Within this model democratic systems were engaged to form a representative government that offered an alternative model to British control.

    Actions of other movements in causing the revolution To evaluate the relative significance of the actions of the Committees of Correspondence, a range of other movements, leaders, events and preconditions could be discussed. There are many options for students to choose from. Other groups and movements as causal factors will be discussed here.

    • 1765: The Sons of Liberty was a secret political organisation that evolved from the Loyal Nine (a Boston-based organisation involved in inciting action against the British and establishing the Liberty Tree in Boston Common). They were primary agitators for acts of resistance against the British and were responsible for organising and executing the 1773 Boston Tea Party. Samuel Adams and John Hancock were members.
    • 1767: The Daughters of Liberty were groups of female patriots whose collective efforts at boycotting British goods and shops and forming gatherings to produce homespun items helped advance the revolutionary cause.
    • 1774: The Minute Men were informally organised groups comprised of militiamen who were ready to take up arms ‘at a minute’s warning’. The 1774 Powder Alarms led to widespread use of the term ‘minutemen’ to describe the rapid mobilisation of colonial forces in constant readiness to march.
    • 1775: The Second Continental Congress voted to form the Continental Army, headed by George Washington.

    Sample student response While a potent combination of ideas, leaders, and political and popular movements caused the American Revolution, the Committees of Correspondence were significant in unifying and amplifying these factors, propelling the colonies towards independence.

    The Committees of Correspondence provided a forum for leaders to communicate and organise united opposition to the British. Groups such as the Sons of Liberty and individuals such as Samuel Adams were already active on this front, but it was the formalisation of the Committees of Correspondence in Boston in 1772 that fostered a greater level of cooperation among revolutionaries. According to Richard D. Brown, the Boston Committee worked with both towns and the House of Representatives to ‘promote aggressively what it regarded as the defense of liberty’. For example, it circulated letters that criticised the 1773 Tea Act and warned other colonies about its implications, which consequently rallied opposition to the British and eventually led to the Boston Tea Party—a key turning point in the American Revolution. This information-sharing resulted in many more coordinated acts of resistance.

    However, other groups and movements were integral in spurring revolutionary fervour among the colonies, whether by agitating for acts of resistance or by boycotting British goods in protest. In the decade preceding 1775, various secret political organisations were established across the colonies to advance the cause of the revolution. Notably, the Loyal Nine, which became the Sons of Liberty, agitated for acts of resistance against the British: they rallied mobs at the Liberty Tree in Boston Common to hang effigies of public officials (Source 2) and later organised the 1773 Boston Tea Party. Similarly, the Daughters of Liberty, a group of female patriots, collectively boycotted British goods and shops by producing their own homespun items, helping to immobilise British imports and ultimately advance the cause for revolution.

    The Committees of Correspondence worked jointly with popular movements to draw on varied levels of support among colonial society. They were able to unite the colonies in a shared ideology among the middle- and upper-classes with their letters, pamphlets and publications.

    D5 MARKSEXPLAIN↩ Restored
    Using Source 3 and your own knowledge, explain the challenges that the American War of Independence posed to the revolutionary government in consolidating its power.
    0 words · aim for ~110
    HTAV 2025/2026 Guide to Responses — suggested discussion points and sample material, not the only acceptable answer.
    • The verb ‘explain’ indicates that students need to provide a structured and logical explanation that clarifies the relationship between concepts or ideas.
    • The question focuses on how the American War of Independence created challenges for the revolutionary government in consolidating its power. Therefore, responses should focus on the consequences of the war and avoid getting sidetracked with its causes or key events.
    • To access the highest marks, students must make meaningful use of Source 3 and incorporate other arguments backed by evidence from their own study.
    Suggested discussion points From Source 3
    • The letter was written by George Washington on 23 December 1777 from the Winter Encampment at Valley Forge. It is addressed to Henry Laurens, who was the president of the Second Continental Congress.
    • ‘Unless some … change suddenly takes place in that line this Army must inevitably be reduced to one or other of these three things. Starve—dissolve—or disperse.’
    • ‘Men were unable to stir on account of provision.’
    • ‘A dangerous mutiny begun the night before and … with difficulty was suppressed by the spirited exertions of some Officers.’
    • ‘The only Commissary … had not a single hoof of any kind to slaughter, and not more than 25 Barrells of Flour!’
    • ‘Three or four days bad weather would prove our destruction.’
    • ‘What then is to become of the Army this Winter?’
    • ‘These are considerations of great magnitude—meriting the closest attention.’
    • ‘Without Provisions now, as with them, what is to become of us in the Spring … to take advantage of an early campaign before the Enemy can be reinforced?’
    From own knowledge
    The American War of Independence
    • The American War of Independence began in 1775 with the battles of Lexington and Concord on 19 April. The war ended on 3 September 1783 with the Treaty of Paris, which resulted in the creation of the United States as an independent nation.
    • The overarching aim of the war was to secure independence from British rule. This was necessary to defeat the British Redcoat forces in their territory and to establish power as a sovereign nation.
    Valley Forge
    • An estimated 11,000 soldiers from the Continental Army camped at Valley Forge from 19 December 1777 to 19 June 1778, to withstand the winter.
    • Around 2500 men did not survive the winter at Valley Forge due to hypothermia and starvation from limited food supplies, requisitioning of locals and unreliable Commissary supply lines.
    • Washington’s letter to Henry Laurens reflects the harsh realities at Valley Forge and the challenges he faced while commanding the Continental Army. Washington served as commander-in-chief from 3 July 1775 for eight years, until his resignation on 23 December 1783.
    • The timing of Washington’s letter (sent 23 December 1777, the day of his resignation) starkly contrasts the victorious nature of his command just one year prior, having successfully led the Continental Army in crossing the Delaware River on 26 December 1776. The Battle of Trenton provided a crucial morale‑boosting victory for the Continental Army over the Hessians.
    Economic, social and political challenges
    • Economically, the letter highlights Washington begging Congress and the colonies for supplies and impelling action to secure financing for the Continental Army.
    • Socially, the Continental Army was made up of men from all 13 colonies aged from as young as 15 up to the age of 40­—with George Washington serving from the ages of 44–52 years. Many of the soldiers were labourers, farmers and tradesmen, including over 5000 African American soldiers.
    • Politically, the Continental Congress was the governing body during the American War of Independence. The letter was specifically addressed to Henry Laurens, president of the Second Continental Congress in 1777, emphasising Congress’s role in supporting the Continental Army.
    • Politically, Congress had to raise an army, engage in diplomacy to secure alliances for support and at crucial times seek local colonial contributions for finance and food supplies.

    Sample student response The American War of Independence (1775–1783) was the defining challenge to the revolutionary government’s consolidation of power and independence from Britain. George Washington’s letter from Valley Forge during the crucial winter of 1777 emphasises the dire situation the Continental Army faced and the depth of its economic and supply challenges, which threatened to ‘starve—dissolve—or disperse’ (Source 3) its soldiers. These logistical issues weakened the army’s morale and effectiveness, encapsulated by Washington’s reference to a ‘dangerous mutiny [that] begun the night before’ (Source 3). Under the Articles of Confederation, the central government lacked the authority to enforce its decisions effectively, hindering its ability to properly fund the war and support its military with men, food and supplies—key ‘considerations of great magnitude—meriting the closest attention’ (Source 3). The government’s inability to take political action to secure allies and re-establish reliable supply lines eroded public confidence, leading to further strains in the consolidation of its power.

    E6 MARKSANALYSE↩ Restored
    Using Source 4 and your own knowledge, analyse how James Madison influenced the development of the new society.
    0 words · aim for ~140
    HTAV 2025/2026 Guide to Responses — suggested discussion points and sample material, not the only acceptable answer.
    • The verb ‘analyse’ indicates that students need to break down each concept into its component parts and explain them separately.
    • To access the highest marks, students must make meaningful use of Source 4 and incorporate other arguments backed by evidence from their own study.
    Suggested discussion points From Source 4
    • The creation of a Bill of Rights was partly spurred by ‘James Madison’s decision to make the speedy adoption of suitable amendments an urgent priority of the First Federal Congress’.
    • ‘Madison receives well deserved credit for his heroic labors in pushing the amendments through an indifferent Congress.’
    • ‘Historians still debate whether even his actions were more … of a campaign conversion prompted by a tough electoral race, … or, alternatively, of a principled reassessment of the value that bills of rights could play in preserving the liberties of republican citizens.’
    • ‘Historians ordinarily tell two kinds of stories about the origins of the Bill of Rights. … Federalists followed from their initial refusal to accept any amendments to the proposed Constitution, to their recognition of the political capital that Antifederalists were gaining through their repeated calls for a Bill of Rights.’
    From own knowledge Father of the Constitution
    • James Madison was coined the ‘Father of the Constitution’ because he laid the foundations for the Great Compromise, having outlined the need for a strong national government with three branches (legislative, executive and judicial) in his Virginia Plan. He also co-wrote The Federalist Papers (1788) with Alexander Hamilton and John Jay, which led to the ratification of the US Constitution in 1788.
    • Madison was the youngest member of the Continental Congress, elected in 1779 at the age of 29. He served as a delegate until 1783.
    • He represented Virginia in Congress during the American Revolution and in the US House of Representatives for eight years.
    • Madison was the fourth president of the United States from 1809–1817.
    Federalist
    • Federalism is a mode of government in which the governing power balance is shared between the national and state governments.
    • Federalism supported a strong, central authoritative government, but balanced this contention by adding a Bill of Rights to the new Constitution.
    • The Federalist Papers (a collection of 85 articles and essays written between October 1787 and May 1788) anchored the debate that led to the ratification of the US Constitution.
    • In particular, Federalist Paper No. 51 highlighted the need for representative democracy, defined the balance of powers and emphasised that ‘the security for civil rights must be the same as that for religious rights’.

    Architect of the Virginia Plan and the Great Compromise (Connecticut Compromise)

    • Madison was a representative for Virginia in the US Congress (hence, the title of the Virginia Plan).
    • The Virginia Plan is significant because it laid the foundation for the Great Compromise (known also as the Connecticut Compromise).
    • The Great Compromise combined elements from two plans:
      • The New Jersey Plan – This plan proposed a single legislative house with an equal number of representatives from each state.
      • The Virginia Plan – This plan proposed two legislative houses (the Senate and the House of Representatives) with equal representation, and three branches of government to separate the powers (legislative, executive and judicial).
    • The Great Compromise achieved a balance between the two plans, establishing two legislative houses with proportional representation in the lower house (House of Representatives) and equal state representation in the upper house (Senate).
    Ideology of separation of powers
    • The separation of powers is emphasised in the Constitution by the legislative, executive and judicial branches of government.
    Author of the Bill of Rights
    • Madison proposed greater religious freedom in the Virginia Declaration of Rights (1776).
    • He argued successfully to change its wording from ‘fullest Toleration [of religion]’ (implying that religions other than the ‘state-approved’ religion were merely tolerated by the government) to ‘free exercise of religion’.
    • Thomas Jefferson’s Virginia Statute for Religious Freedom, which was passed 10 years later in 1786, outlines the separation of church and state. (This was later key for the First Amendment in the Constitution, beginning with a Bill of Rights.)
    • The Bill of Rights comprises the first 10 amendments added to the Constitution in 1791.

    Sample student response James Madison’s leadership in drafting and advocating for a Bill of Rights greatly shaped the new society. As historian Irving Brant describes, Madison ‘did the most’ but is ‘known the least’. Firstly, Madison was the architect of the Virginia Plan (1787), which formed the basis for the Great Compromise during the Constitutional Convention of 1787. This plan proposed a strong national government with a bicameral legislature, where representation was based on state population or financial contributions. Many of its ideas were included in the final draft of the US Constitution, further highlighting its significance and Madison’s influence. Secondly, Madison is credited with writing 29 of the 85 Federalist Papers (1788), which advocated for a strong federal government, a key factor in the ratification of the Constitution—hence, the moniker ‘Father of the Constitution’. Finally, as Source 4 describes, Madison changed his stance on the Bill of Rights, making suitable amendments a ‘priority of the First Federal Congress’. This proved politically astute, ‘preserving the liberties of republican citizens’ (Source 4) and limiting the government’s powers while appeasing the Anti-Federalists. The Bill of Rights, added in 1791, further underscored Madison’s skill in compromise and his impact.

    Question 2 (25 marks) · The French Revolution

    Read Sources 5–8 below, then answer parts a–e.

    Source 5

    A historical interpretation, published in 2016, of the 1788 harvest crisis in France in the lead-up to the revolution.

    In 1788, a ruinous harvest crisis hit most of the kingdom. The summer had been characterised by long, dry periods, followed by wild storms. Thomas Blaikie, a famous Scottish gardener employed by Louis-Philippe-Joseph d’Orleans (Louis XVI’s cousin) on his 800-acre estate ten miles east of Paris at Le Raincy, noted how huge hailstones had sliced through branches and killed ‘hares, partridges and many other things’. At the southern extreme of the kingdom, in the Corbières, hail and rain swelled at the River Verdouble to a point where it carried away part of the bridge at Rouffiac, ruined hundreds of acres of millet1 and beans, and washed away 1200 hay-ricks2, in all about half the year’s produce.

    Source: Peter McPhee, Liberty or Death: The French Revolution (New Haven: Yale University Press, 2016), 54–55.

    1. millet – a cereal crop that produces a large amount of small grains
    2. hay-ricks – a barn or shed used for storing hay
    Source 6

    This cartoon titled ‘In Times Past, Even the Most Useful Were Trampled Underfoot’ was published in France in 1789. It shows a French peasant being crushed under a boulder, on which two members of the privileged orders stand.

    The text on the boulder reads ‘taille1, impôts2 and corvée3’.

    1. taille – the main land tax that peasants had to pay
    2. impôts – general taxes
    3. corvée – the obligation of the peasants to perform unpaid labour for their lord, particularly on roads
    Source 7

    A historical interpretation, published in 2021, of the Marquis de Lafayette’s involvement in the Champ de Mars Massacre on 17 July 1791.

    Lafayette and some National Guard companies arrived in the afternoon and ordered the crowd to disperse. When they were ignored, Lafayette and his men regrouped and waited for reinforcements. At around seven o’clock in the evening, Bailly appeared with more men, waving the red flag of martial law1 and repeating the order to disperse. … The National Guard fired directly into the crowd. … People ran in every direction as shots rang out. It was all over in a few bloody, noisy, confusing minutes. Lafayette and Bailly returned their companies to disciplined order. They succeeded in dispersing the crowd, but at what cost?

    Source: Mike Duncan, Hero of Two Worlds: The Marquis de Lafayette in the Age of Revolution (New York: PublicAffairs, 2021), 276.

    1. the red flag of martial law – a red flag that was waved to indicate that the crowd had to disperse immediately or risk being fired upon
    Source 8

    An extract from the Declaration of Pillnitz, issued on 27 August 1791 in the name of Leopold II, Emperor of Austria, and William II, King of Prussia. It highlights the hostility of foreign powers towards the French Revolution.

    His Majesty the Emperor1 and His Majesty the King of Prussia2 … jointly declare that they regard the present position of His Majesty the King of France as a matter of common concern to all the sovereigns of Europe. They trust that the powers whose aid is supplicated3 will not fail to recognise this fact; and that, accordingly, they will not refuse to co-operate with the said Majesties in employing, in proportion to their forces, the most effective means enabling the King of France to consolidate with complete freedom the foundations of a monarchical government, equally suited to the rights of sovereigns and the welfare of the French nation. In which case their said Majesties, the Emperor and the King of Prussia, are resolved to act promptly, in mutual accord4, with the forces necessary to attain the proposed common objective.

    Source: Mark Fielding and Margot Morcombe, The Spirit of Change: France in Revolution (Sydney: McGraw Hill, 2003), 93.

    1. His Majesty the Emperor – Leopold II
    2. His Majesty the King of Prussia – William II
    3. supplicated – asked for
    4. mutual accord – common or shared agreement
    A2 MARKSLIST↩ Restored
    List two consequences of the harvest crisis highlighted in Source 5.
    0 words · aim for ~25
    HTAV 2025/2026 Guide to Responses — suggested discussion points and sample material, not the only acceptable answer.
    • The verb ‘list’ indicates that students can simply give a numbered list of two short, direct quotations from Source 5.
    • No explanation or analysis is required.
    • Students could refer to any two of the consequences below.
    Suggested discussion points/sample response
    • A Scottish gardener noticed how ‘huge hailstones’ broke branches and killed small animals on Louis XVI’s cousin’s estate.
    • The rain damaged vital infrastructure, such as ‘part of the bridge at Rouffiac’.
    • It also damaged farmland and agriculture, including ‘hundreds of acres of millet and beans’.
    • Overall, ‘about half the year’s produce’ was lost due to the storm.
    B3 MARKSOUTLINE↩ Restored
    Outline how Source 6 depicts the grievances of the peasantry prior to the revolution.
    0 words · aim for ~50
    HTAV 2025/2026 Guide to Responses — suggested discussion points and sample material, not the only acceptable answer.
    • The verb ‘outline’ indicates that students should give a high-level overview or summary of the main ideas. This will work best with concise, full sentences.
    • There is no requirement for students to use their own knowledge. It is possible to achieve full marks using the source alone. However, some students may choose to draw on their own knowledge to contextualise or expand on ideas in the source.
    • As the question is worth 3 marks, it would be appropriate for students to discuss any three of the features of the image.
    Suggested discussion points
    • The peasants’ grievances are represented by multiple features in Source 6:
      • A peasant is lying on the ground with a large boulder on his chest, which reads ‘taille, impôts and corvée’. This refers to the various taxes that French peasants had to pay the Crown and their lords.
      • Two members of the privileged estates stand on top of the boulder: a member of the clergy is depicted on the left, and a member of the nobility is on the right.
      • The clergyman appears to be offering a blessing to the peasant, but he is not helping. He represents the tithe paid by peasants to the Catholic Church.
      • The nobleman seems to be indifferent to the plight of the peasant. His sword is a symbol of his power and authority, as well as the coercive measures used to keep the peasants under control. He represents the feudal dues owed by peasants to their lords.
    C9 MARKSEVALUATE↩ Restored
    Evaluate the significance of the Night of Patriotic Delirium as a cause of revolution. Use evidence to support your response.
    0 words · aim for ~220
    HTAV 2025/2026 Guide to Responses — suggested discussion points and sample material, not the only acceptable answer.
    • The command term for this question is ‘evaluate’. This means that students should aim to form a judgement.
    • The question asks students to explore the significance of the Night of Patriotic Delirium. That is, rather than simply describing what happened, students should form arguments about why the event can be seen as important in bringing about a revolution.
    • Strong responses will meaningfully explore the extent to which the Night of Patriotic Delirium caused the revolution. However, it may be appropriate to argue that this was not the most significant factor and to develop a counterargument that other factors, such as the Great Fear and the storming of the Bastille, were more significant.
    Suggested discussion points Significance of the Night of Patriotic Delirium
    • The Night of Patriotic Delirium (4–5 August 1789) played a key role in securing the overthrow of the ancien régime in France.
    • Responding to news from the countryside that there was a nationwide peasant uprising (the Great Fear), the deputies of the National Constituent Assembly knew they had to respond.
    • It was necessary to quell the uprising to ensure that peasants could collect the harvest, which would help lower the cost of flour and bread in the cities and, in turn, appease the urban workers.
    • Options considered by the deputies included using the army to suppress the peasants, but the deputies felt that this might lead to civil war or return too much power to King Louis XVI.
    • A group of deputies from Brittany, who called themselves the Breton Club, decided that a different approach which did not involve the use of force was required.
    • They approached one of the highest members of the peerage in France, the Duc d’Aiguillon, to mount the rostrum at the Assembly on the night of 4–5 August and voluntarily renounce his privileges. It was hoped that this would encourage other noble deputies to come forward and do the same.
    • That way the feudal system and its privileges—a significant cause of peasant unrest and grievance—would be abolished without violence. The peasants would be appeased, and the nobility would be able to retain the material aspects of their wealth (i.e., property and land rented out to peasants).
    • However, before d’Aiguillon could take the stage, the Vicomte de Noailles (a French nobleman) rushed out and renounced his privileges first. The Duc could only second the motion.
    • This started what the Marquis de Ferrières, another deputy, called the night of ‘patriotic drunkenness’, during which noble deputies rose to rostrum and renounced their privileges and rights. The members of the upper clergy did the same.
    • By that evening, the centuries-old feudal system of France had been brought to an end. It needed only to be ratified by a decree from the Assembly to become legal.

    Other factors that contributed to revolution in France To evaluate the relative significance of the Night of Patriotic Delirium, a range of other events, leaders and preconditions should be discussed. There are many options for students to choose from. Two important causal factors will be discussed here: the Great Fear, and the storming of the Bastille.

    The Great Fear
    • There would have been no need to appease the peasants had there been no general peasant uprising. Historian Georges Lefebvre has called this the ‘Great Fear’.
    • The French peasantry had long laboured under the feudal system. This system gave hereditary privileges and exemptions to a tiny proportion of French society: the nobility.
    • The nobles were largely exempt from paying taxes. They had hunting rights and a range of other privileges. The peasantry owed them a range of feudal dues that were written down on terrier (legal documents outlining a peasant’s obligations to their lord).
    • The peasants also owed the corvée to their lord. This involved labouring on local roads. The corvée was unpaid and took peasants away from working on their own fields.
    • Peasants also owed a range of direct and indirect taxes to the Crown and the tithe to the Catholic Church.
    • In addition, periodic harvest crises and food shortages meant that peasants could not afford to eat and so starved. Many turned to begging or theft to survive.
    • There had been peasant revolts in the countryside since 1788, which intensified in the summer of 1789. As food supplies began to dwindle, peasants attacked stores of grain and let their animals graze on the lords’ land.
    • According to Lefebvre, the Great Fear was distinct from typical peasant uprisings. After the storming of the Bastille, peasants believed that the nobility would take revenge by hiring ‘brigands’ or foreign soldiers to crush the rebellion. The term ‘brigands’ was used by the revolutionaries to describe those who opposed the revolution, and later encompassed all anti-revolutionary groups. Labelling them as such allowed the revolutionaries to justify the harsh measures and unlawful killings against them.
    • In anticipation, peasants armed themselves with whatever weapons they could find and waited. When the ‘brigands’ failed to materialise, the peasantry across France took out their anxieties and frustration on their local lord.
    • The peasants attacked symbols of the feudal nobility, such as doves, rabbits, deer, heraldry, weathervanes, the chateaux, and the terrier, which recorded the peasants’ obligation to their lord.
    • While some chateaux were burnt to the ground, there was very little physical violence against individuals.
    • Reports of the generalised peasant revolt reached the National Assembly. The deputies were deeply concerned about the attacks on property. They were determined to quell the uprising and re-establish order across the countryside.
    The storming of the Bastille
    • The urban workers of Paris also revolted in mid-July 1789 in opposition to the king’s response to the formation of a National Assembly.
    • Bread prices had been rising since the hailstorm of July 1788. By the summer of 1789, bread had reached 14 sous per loaf, which was almost a full day’s pay for most unskilled labourers.
    • The rising cost of living and unemployment pushed the urban workers to the edge. They believed that Louis XVI was conjuring troops to the Paris–Versailles region to shut down the Estates-General to keep bread prices high so he could pay off the national debt. This became known as the ‘bread plot’.
    • The workers revolted on 12 July 1789, seizing weapons to defend the capital from royal soldiers. Their capture of the Bastille on 14 July 1789 signalled that the king had lost control of his capital and his army. He essentially relinquished legislative authority to the National Assembly the next day.

    Sample student response While the Night of Patriotic Delirium (4–5 August 1789) undoubtedly played a role in ending the feudal system in France, other events were necessary to catalyse the revolution and transfer authority from the king to the National Assembly.

    Prior to the French Revolution, the social system of France granted only a tiny noble minority with special rights and privileges. In response to the nationwide peasant uprisings known as the Great Fear, on the night of 4–5 August 1789 the aristocratic deputies rushed to renounce their privileges in what the Marquis de Ferrières called a night of ‘patriotic drunkenness’. This included multiple rights concerning fiscal exemptions, hunting and their own law courts. Members of the clergy were also encouraged to discard privileges such as collecting the tithe. Historian William Doyle describes the evening as ‘the most sweeping and radical legislative session of the whole French Revolution’.

    However, the Night of Patriotic Delirium would not have occurred without the initial peasant uprisings. Called the ‘Great Fear’ by Georges Lefebvre, this was a nationwide peasant revolt against feudal dues and the high price of food. More specifically, it was a reaction to the fear that the nobility had hired brigands and foreign troops to crush the peasantry. From late July to early August, peasants shot and ate the lords’ game, destroyed any symbols denoting nobility and burnt the terriers (the lists of feudal dues kept in the lords’ chateaux). Finally, the storming of the Bastille secured the political transformation of absolutist France into a constitutional monarchy. Suffering from severely high bread prices and believing that the king was about to close the Estates‑General by force, the Parisian crowd rose up and stormed the Bastille on 14 July 1789. This demonstrated that Louis had lost effective control of his army, and he was forced to transfer legislative authority to the National Assembly.

    Hence, while the Night of Patriotic Delirium played a key role in ending feudalism in France, other events such as the Great Fear and the storming of the Bastille were crucial episodes in the transformation of French society.

    D6 MARKSANALYSE↩ Restored
    Using Source 7 and your own knowledge, analyse how the Marquis de Lafayette influenced the development of the new society.
    0 words · aim for ~140
    HTAV 2025/2026 Guide to Responses — suggested discussion points and sample material, not the only acceptable answer.
    • The verb ‘analyse’ indicates that students need to break down each concept into its component parts and explain them separately.
    • To access the highest marks, students must make meaningful use of Source 7 and incorporate other arguments backed by evidence from their own study.
    Suggested discussion points From Source 7
    • On the day of the Champ de Mars Massacre, Lafayette and the National Guard ‘ordered the crowd to disperse’.
    • The crowd refused, even though Bailly, the mayor of Paris, ‘[waved] the red flag of martial law’.
    • The order was given, and the ‘National Guard fired directly into the crowd’.
    • In the ensuing chaos, the National Guard ‘succeeded in dispersing the crowd’.
    • The political ‘cost’ for the revolution, and Lafayette personally, was immense.

    From own knowledge Lafayette played an important role at key moments in the revolution that either won his great support or garnered the hatred of his political enemies.

    • Lafayette participated in drafting the Declaration of the Rights of Man and Citizen (26 August 1789), which was one of the foundation documents of the revolution.
    • He reluctantly accompanied the crowd and his own National Guard troops to Versailles on 5–6 October 1789. He managed to calm down the crowd and probably saved the lives of the royal family.
    • After the Champ de Mars Massacre, Lafayette resigned (October 1791) as commander of the National Guard.
    • As war with Austria seemed increasingly likely, Louis XVI appointed Lafayette to command one of the three new French armies on the frontier.
    • In an effort to save the monarchy, Lafayette made a speech before the Assembly (28 June 1792), where he called for all political clubs to be closed down and freedom of the press restricted.
    • This failed, and Lafayette returned to his army in Alsace. On 17 August 1792, he was dismissed from his position as commander of the National Guard and, fearing for his life, defected to the Austrian army.
    • This only confirmed the suspicions of the radical revolutionaries that ex‑nobles could not be trusted and that they were actively working towards restoring Louis to the throne. This pushed France closer towards the Terror.

    Sample student response The Marquis de Lafayette inadvertently played a key role in the development of a new society that favoured radicalism over moderation. He helped draft the Declaration of the Rights of Man and Citizen (26 August 1789) which articulated the founding principles of the revolution, and reluctantly accompanied the National Guard on the October Days (5–6 October 1789), possibly saving the royal family from the Paris mob. However, any political support he possessed was soon spent. On 17 July 1791, the National Guard, which Lafayette commanded, fired ‘directly into the crowd’ (Source 7) of Parisians who were signing a petition for a republic in the wake of Louis XVI’s flight from Paris (20–21 June 1791). While the Guardsmen ‘succeeded in dispersing the crowd’, the unity of the early stages of the revolution was broken. Commanding a French army on the frontier during the war with Austria and Prussia, Lafayette demanded the closure of political clubs. Fearing a royalist-military coup, the Assembly dismissed him. Lafayette then defected to the Austrian army, confirming fears of the reactionary nobility and pushing France further towards the Terror.

    E5 MARKSEXPLAIN↩ Restored
    Using Source 8 and your own knowledge, explain the challenges that the hostility of foreign powers posed to the revolutionary government in consolidating its power.
    0 words · aim for ~110
    HTAV 2025/2026 Guide to Responses — suggested discussion points and sample material, not the only acceptable answer.
    • The verb ‘explain’ indicates that students need to provide a structured and logical explanation that clarifies the relationship between concepts or ideas.
    • The question focuses on how the hostility of foreign powers created challenges for the revolutionary government in consolidating its power. Therefore, responses should focus on the consequences of the hostility and avoid getting sidetracked with the causes.
    • To access the highest marks, students must make meaningful use of Source 8 and incorporate other arguments backed by evidence from their own study.
    Suggested discussion points From Source 8
    • The Emperor of Austria and King of Prussia declared that the plight of Louis XVI was ‘a matter of common concern to all the sovereigns of Europe’.
    • They pledged to find ‘the most effective means’ of supporting ‘with complete freedom the foundations of a monarchical government’.
    • The emperor and king sought to restore ‘the rights of sovereigns and the welfare of the French nation’.
    • They also ‘resolved to act promptly … with the forces necessary to attain the proposed common objective’.
    From own knowledge
    • Deeply concerned over the fate of his brother-in-law and the potential spread of revolutionary ideas across Europe, Emperor Leopold II held the Mantua Conference (20 May 1791) and the Padua Circular (6 July 1791). While these called for a restoration of Louis XVI’s authority and a limit to the spread of revolutionary sentiment, no statement of action was made.
    • A joint statement was issued by Leopold II and King Frederick William II of Prussia, known as the Declaration of Pillnitz (27 August 1791). This represented a much clearer threat of action against the revolution, but did not specify what or when.
    • Rather than intimidate the revolutionaries, it only emboldened them. Jacques‑Pierre Brissot, a deputy in the Legislative Assembly, gave a speech on 14 October 1791 arguing that foreign powers were seeking to restore Louis’s full authority.
    • The mounting tension with foreign powers culminated in France declaring war on Austria and Prussia in April 1792.
    • The French armies did poorly in the initial stages of the war, with ex‑noble officers defecting and the armies on the frontier retreating.
    • The Prussian army advanced through France and issued the Brunswick Manifesto (25 July 1792). This threatened to destroy Paris and eliminate revolutionaries if the royal family were harmed in any way. This prompted the storming of the Tuileries on 10 August 1792 and the declaration of a republic.
    • The threat posed by the Prussians was realised when the French fortresses of Verdun and Longwy fell quickly in August 1792. The consequent panic in Paris resulted in the September Massacres.
    • The French government declared war on Britain, Spain and Holland in February 1793. Known as the War of the First Coalition, this conflict saw France surrounded by enemies on all sides.
    • The summer of 1793 was particularly desperate for the revolutionary government. The British fleet had blockaded French ports, and foreign armies had crossed French borders from every direction.
    • The Mediterranean port of Toulon surrendered to the British in September 1793. Half of the French Mediterranean fleet was lost to the enemy.
    • Only extraordinary measures, such as the declaration of total war via a levée en masse (mass national conscription) in August 1793, could defend France from its external enemies.
    • The Battle of Fleurus (26 July 1794) saw France defeat an Austrian army and protect the gains of the revolution.
    • Students might also want to mention the papal bull Charitas. Issued by Pope Pius VI in April 1791, this document forbade any member of the Catholic clergy in France to swear the Clerical Oath. The penalty was excommunication (official exclusion from a Christian church). Such hostility from Pope Pius VI caused significant turmoil in France as devout Catholics chose their religion over the revolution.

    Sample student response Foreign powers posed a great threat to the revolutionary government in consolidating its power throughout the French Revolution. One challenge followed the Mantua Conference (May 1791) and the Padua Circular (July 1791), where Austrian Emperor Leopold II tried to rally nations for a military intervention against the revolution. A more direct threat came from King Frederick William II of Prussia in the Declaration of Pillnitz (27 August 1791), which ‘resolved to act promptly … with the forces necessary’ (Source 8) to restore the rights of Louis XVI. However, this only fuelled hostility among the revolutionaries who, led by Brissot, declared war on Austria and Prussia in April 1792. The war initially went badly for France, with the Duke of Brunswick issuing a manifesto in July 1792 threatening to destroy the city. The War of the First Coalition (February 1793) threatened to overwhelm the French Republic, and the revolution was only able to survive by resorting to the most desperate measures.

    Section B — Essay

    Write an essay on one of the following. The 20-mark essay is assessed against the criteria below.

    Question 1 (20 marks) · The American Revolution
    ESSAY20 MARKS↩ Restored
    ‘Although the ideas of Representative Government and Republicanism drove the American Revolution, they were ultimately compromised in the Constitution of the United States.’

    To what extent do you agree? Use evidence to support your response.
    0 words · aim for ~700
    HTAV 2025/2026 Guide to Responses — suggested discussion points and sample material, not the only acceptable answer.
    Suggested discussion points
    • This question presents an interpretation of both a cause of the American Revolution (that the ideas of Representative Government and Republicanism drove the revolution) and an interpretation of a consequence of the American Revolution (that the ideas of Representative Government and Republicanism were compromised in the Constitution).
    • Strong essays will meaningfully explore both parts of the interpretation.
    • Strong essays will form a clear contention. They may:
      • accept both propositions
      • accept one proposition but reject or qualify the other
      • reject both propositions.
    • Strong essays will stay firmly focused on the ideas of Representative Government and Republicanism.

    Possible discussion points that support the view in the question Students can argue that ‘the idea of Representative Government drove the American Revolution’ by exploring the following:

    • The ideas driving the American Revolution were influenced by Enlightenment thinkers such as John Locke and Montesquieu. One key idea from the Enlightenment was Representative Government, wherein people elect leaders to represent them and act on their behalf. Locke pointed to the two houses in the British Parliament: one that is elected by the people (the House of Commons), and one made up of hereditary (or inherited) positions (the House of Lords).
    • Ideology and colonial belief in representation was emblazoned as a catchcry of the revolution with the slogan ‘No taxation without representation’. James Otis coined the phrase in 1761 to condemn the British writs of assistance and later explored its meaning in the 1763 pamphlet The Rights of British Colonies Asserted and Proved.
    • Otis also documented and advanced the notion of Representative Government in this pamphlet and explored the idea of direct representation as a unifying cause for revolution: ‘The colonies [should] be also represented in some proportion to their number and estates, in the grand legislature of the nation.’
    • The agitation for a representative government was a long-term issue that was accelerated by trigger events such as the 1765 Stamp Act and the 1773 Tea Act.
    • Colonists had direct representation as landowners, with an estimated 75 per cent of men being eligible to vote. Elected representatives were to live in the electorate. This experience defined their case for direct representation by those living among them, representing both local and shared needs.
    • Statements from British parliamentarians emphasise the division of belief on representation between British rule and colonial desire. For example, in developing the doctrine of ‘virtual representation’ (wherein the elected body has the authority to speak for the interests of all citizens), British politician Thomas Whately stated that ‘colonists, like those individuals and groups who resided in Britain but had no voice in elections, were nonetheless virtually represented in Parliament’ (Greene).

    Students can argue that ‘the idea of Republicanism drove the American Revolution’ by exploring the following:

    • Revolutionary ideology linked Representative Government and Republicanism.
    • People in colonial America increasingly demanded equal representation in government. The notions of colonial unity, a national focus and the desire for actual representation over virtual representation define early colonial ideas of Republicanism.
    • Republicanism as an Enlightenment idea can be attributed to the writing of Montesquieu, who highlighted the importance of a national constitution and the need for the separation of powers.
    • A distillation of Republicanism was further advanced by the concept of a government without a monarch, as defined in Thomas Paine’s 1776 pamphlet Common Sense, in which he advocated for ‘a republic: a state without a king.’ This idea of Republicanism hinged on the notion of popular sovereignty and abandoning the tradition of a hereditary monarch.
    • Republicanism as an idea that encompasses national unity is evidenced in a statement made by a member of the Virginia House of Burgess in 1774, in response to the Coercive Acts: ‘An attack made on one of our sister colonies … is an attack made on all British America.’
    • Republicanism is also evident in the Declaration of Independence (1776):
      • ‘The history of the present King of Great Britain is a history of repeated injuries and usurpations.’
      • ‘In every stage of these Oppressions We have Petitioned for Redress in the most humble terms: Our repeated Petitions have been answered only by repeated injury. A Prince whose character is thus marked by every act which may define a Tyrant, is unfit to be the ruler of a free people.’
    • These excerpts highlight the colonies’ decision to break away from British rule, and further emphasise the failure of peaceful negotiation and the need for independence from a monarch in King George III.

    Students can argue that ‘the ideas of Representative Government and Republicanism were compromised in the Constitution’ by exploring the following:

    • Members of colonial society were not represented in the Constitution.
    • Rights and representation were alien to African Americans, First Nations peoples, Loyalists and women.
    • Historian Charles Beard identifies ‘four groups [that] were not represented in the Constitutional Convention: slaves, indentured servants and women, [and] men without property’ (quoted in Zinn).
    • Women were not represented directly but played a role in the new democratic Republicanism.
    • Constitutional Conventions held in Annapolis, Maryland (1786), and Philadelphia, Pennsylvania (1787), reflected the compromise of these ideals.
    • Anti-Federalists argued that the Constitution did not fully reflect the principles of Representative Government and failed to explicitly protect individual rights. They demanded a Bill of Rights, which proposed 12 amendments to the Constitution to safeguard individual liberties. Their efforts aimed to preserve Natural Rights, freedom of religion and freedom of speech.
    • The Three-Fifths Compromise provides a key example of how the ideas of Representative Government and Republicanism were undermined during the revolution.
      • The compromise was reached between state delegates during the Constitutional Convention of 1787.
      • It determined that three out of every five slaves were counted when determining a state’s total population for legislative representation and taxation.
      • This had direct effects on the number of seats in the House of Representatives, as it was determined by the state’s total population.
      • As a result of this clause, southern states held more seats in the House of Representatives, claiming 30 out of 65 seats in Congress.

    Possible discussion points that challenge the view in the question Students can challenge the claim that ‘the ideas of Representative Government and Republicanism drove the American Revolution’ by exploring other ideas that may have contributed more.

    • Enlightenment thinkers such as John Locke spurred the notion that human beings were equal in their ‘natural rights to life, liberty and property’. These ideas became key building blocks in developing the US Constitution.
    • Patrick Henry promoted the idea of Natural Rights—rights that are universal and inalienable and that deem all human beings as equals—in the Virginia Resolves of 1765. He believed that colonists were ‘entitled to all liberties, privileges and immunities … as if they had been abiding and born within the Realm of England’.
    • The Natural Rights of liberty and freedom formed an extended ideological framework on which the colonists could resist British oppression in economic, social and political realms.
    • Key British legislation enflamed tensions between the colonies and Great Britain.
    • Notably, the writs of assistance and the Townshend Duties asserted British authority over the colonies and infringed on personal liberties and property rights.
    • Colonists felt a sense of oppression due to the presence of a British standing army in the colonies.
    • This sense of oppression was also present in a range of Acts passed by the British government.
    • Economic control and taxation policies imposed by the British presented a direct threat to colonists’ prosperity and freedoms, particularly the passage of the Stamp Act (1765) and the Coercive Acts (1774).
    • The Declaration of Independence (1776)—the definitive case for revolutionary idealism written primarily by Thomas Jefferson—outlined the concepts of ‘unalienable Rights’ and ‘Life, Liberty and the Pursuit of Happiness’.
    • These laid the ideological foundation for the colonies’ decision to break away from Britain and assert the peoples’ right to self-government.

    Students can challenge the claim that ‘the ideas of Representative Government and Republicanism were ultimately compromised in the Constitution’ by exploring the process involved in crafting the features of the Constitution.

    • Representative Government:
      • The 1787 Philadelphia Convention was a key event in the development of ideas about Representative Government and Republicanism. These concepts helped to define a new ideological framework for government.
      • Models of representation in government were developed during debates between Federalists and Anti-Federalists at the 1787 and 1788 Constitutional Conventions.
      • These debates became a significant feature in crafting what would become the US Constitution.
    • Federalists:
      • Key Federalists include James Madison and Alexander Hamilton.
      • Eighty-five Federalist Papers were published between 1787 and 1788. These papers engaged colonists in the intellectual, ideological and pragmatic factors that drove the creation of a constitution.
      • Federalist models emphasised a strong, central national government.
      • They wanted: ▪ three branches of government (legislative, executive and judicial) ▪ a president and a strong executive ▪ a bicameral legislature (two-house system of government).
    • Anti-Federalists:
      • Key Anti-Federalists include Patrick Henry, Thomas Jefferson and Samuel Adams.
      • Anti-Federalists endorsed a Republican model, which gave states total sovereignty to prevent the rise of tyrannical government and to limit the power of an executive branch.
      • Anti-Federalists did not want a president. They wanted: ▪ state sovereignty ▪ a unicameral legislature (one-house system of government).
      • The Anti-Federalist movement emphasised the need to maintain individual rights enshrined in the Constitution, as this would keep the power of a central government in check.
    • Representative Government as represented in government plans:
      • Plans proposed at the 1787 Constitutional Convention reflected the name of the state and its size and which side of the debate a government plan represented. An analysis of whether the ideas of the revolution were compromised in the Constitution is measured here using the Great Compromise. ▪ The Virginia Plan was a Federalist plan that proposed a two-house system of government, where representation in both houses was based on population (protecting the interest and representation of large states). ▪ The New Jersey Plan was an Anti-Federalist plan that proposed a one‑house system of government, where representation was equal for each state (protecting the interests and representation of small states). ▪ The Great Compromise combined these two plans and established a two‑house system of government. This comprised a lower house (House of Representatives), with representation based on population (note the Three‑fifths Compromise here), and an upper house (Senate), composed of two senators from each state.
      • Each plan emphasised the competing elements of state representation as a key element in refining the Constitution.
    • Republicanism and the separation of powers:
      • In revolutionary America, Republicanism encompassed a political ideology that hinged on the political separation from Britain and the establishment of a free, sovereign nation.
      • At the Philadelphia Convention (1787), Hamilton stated that ‘we are now forming a republican government. Real liberty is neither found in despotism or the extremes of democracy, but in moderate governments.’
      • The Convention refined the ideology into a tangible model of government and established Republicanism. It defined checks and balances, which was a contemporary and nuanced concept for 1787.
      • Power was defined in terms of three branches of government, each with the ability to power-check the other branches.
      • Thomas Jefferson and John Adams were key advocates for the separation of powers.
      • Jefferson wrote to John Adams advocating for the model: ‘The first principle of good government is … a distribution of its power into executive, judiciary and legislative.’
      • The Constitution officially established three separate but equal branches of government: ▪ The executive branch: headed by the president ▪ The legislative branch: Congress ▪ The judicial branch: the courts
      • Checks and balances were introduced to control power and inhibit tyranny.
      • The executive branch is checked by: ▪ the Supreme Court, as presidential orders can be declared unconstitutional by law ▪ the Senate, which can impeach the president and approves presidential appointments ▪ Congress, which approves presidential raising of revenue and presidential declarations of war.
      • The legislative branch is checked by: ▪ the president, who can veto legislation and convene Congress in an emergency as commander-in-chief ▪ the Supreme Court, which can rule legislation unconstitutional.
      • The judicial branch is checked by: ▪ Congress, which can alter the number of sitting justices on the Supreme Court and can impeach both Supreme and lower court justices ▪ the Senate, which can approve judicial appointments ▪ the president, who holds the authority and can issue pardons.

    Sample student response The ideas of Representative Government and Republicanism were critical driving forces of the American Revolution, though they were partially compromised in the US Constitution. Colonial agitation from 1763–1776 for actual representation in government featured in revolutionary ideology. Early stages of revolutionary ideas included Locke’s ‘natural rights to life, liberty and property’ and were followed by concepts of Republicanism in the 1776 pamphlet Common Sense and the Declaration of Independence. In the crafting and eventual ratification of the Constitution by 4 March 1789, ideology was the focus of debate among leaders, central to the publication of many papers and integral to political compromise. The Constitution enshrined the key elements of Republicanism and, although contested and refined, Representative Government was also represented in the framework of government.

    Representation was an early and enduring idea in the case for revolution. Patrick Henry’s 1765 Virginia Resolves asserted that colonists were entitled to ‘all liberties, privileges and immunities … as if they had been abiding and born within the Realm of England’. Foundational to this assertion was James Otis’s notion of direct representation, where the colonies would be ‘represented in some proportion to their number and estates, in the grand legislature of the nation’. This emphasis on direct representation highlights the colonists’ rejection of ‘virtual representation’ in Parliament and laid the groundwork for their demand that any legitimate government must derive its authority from the consent of the governed. Republican ideals also gained traction during this period, with Thomas Paine’s Common Sense (1776) advocating for a state without a king. Paine famously stated that monarchy was unfit for a free people, and the Declaration of Independence furthered this sentiment, condemning King George III’s ‘usurpations’ and arguing for self-rule.

    The ideological foundations of the new nation were established at the 1787 Constitutional Convention in Philadelphia, and a model of Republicanism emerged. Montesquieu’s Enlightenment idea of Republicanism included the separation of powers. This separation is reflected in a letter from Thomas Jefferson to John Adams, in which he states that ‘the first principle of good government is … a distribution of its power into executive, judiciary and legislative [branches]’. This desire to establish equilibrium in governance was included in the design of the Constitution through the separation of powers and checks and balances; these were necessary to control power and limit tyranny in a republican government. To ensure these principles of fair governance, the Constitution defined three branches of government: executive (the president), legislative (Senate and Congress), and judiciary (Supreme Court). Each branch played a role within this system of checks and balances, to limit the power of a centralised authority. For example, though the president can veto legislation and convene Congress in an emergency as commander-in-chief, the Supreme Court can rule legislation unconstitutional. The enduring legacy of Republicanism ideas are evident in this structure.

    The 1787 Philadelphia Convention also saw debates over Representative Government that would come to shape the framework of the new Constitution. This period featured Federalists, Anti-Federalists and the three government plans that unpacked the elements of what state representation would mean in the Constitution. Representative Government for Federalists such as Alexander Hamilton featured a strong, central national government with two houses for representation. This bicameral model included three branches of government with a president heading the executive branch. In contrast, Representative Government for Anti-Federalists such as Patrick Henry emphasised state sovereignty over a strong central government. This unicameral system, which featured only one house, was central to their model of representation. In June 1787, two plans were tabled to reflect these competing frameworks. These opposing proposals were resolved in July 1787 with the Connecticut Plan, or the Great Compromise. This established a bicameral legislature: the House of Representatives, based on population, and the Senate, with two representatives per state, balancing both perspectives.

    Though compromises were made in finalising the Constitution, the revolutionary ideals of Representative Government and Republicanism were ultimately enshrined in the final body of laws that came to be the US Constitution. This was chiefly possible thanks to those who ‘never abandoned the belief … of a republican state’ where ‘sufficient virtue existed to sustain the American Republic’ (Bailyn).

    Question 2 (20 marks) · The French Revolution
    ESSAY20 MARKS↩ Restored
    ‘Although women played a key role in the events that caused and maintained the French Revolution, they received few benefits in the new regime.’

    To what extent do you agree? Use evidence to support your response.
    0 words · aim for ~700
    HTAV 2025/2026 Guide to Responses — suggested discussion points and sample material, not the only acceptable answer.
    Suggested discussion points
    • This question presents an interpretation of both a cause of the French Revolution (that women played a key role in the events that caused the revolution) and an interpretation of a consequence of the French Revolution (that women received few benefits in the new regime).
    • Strong essays will meaningfully explore both parts of the interpretation.
    • Strong essays will form a clear contention. They may:
      • accept both propositions
      • accept one proposition but reject or qualify the other
      • reject both propositions.
    • Strong essays will stay firmly focused on women.

    Possible discussion points that support the view in the question Students can argue that ‘women played a key role in the events that caused and maintained the French Revolution’ by exploring their actions in safeguarding the revolution.

    • Although the narrative of the course of the revolution is dominated by men, ‘women at crucial points were of decisive importance’ (William Doyle).
    • One woman (Marie Charpentier) was recognised by the Assembly as a conqueror of the Bastille.
    • Women played a much more significant role in the October Days:
      • On 5–6 October 1789, approximately 6000 working-class women from the market district of Paris marched to Versailles to present their grievances to the king and bring the royal family back to Paris.
      • This was due to high bread prices and suspicions that the king was not sincere in his support for the revolution.
      • The women secured the king’s assent for the August Decrees and the Declaration of the Rights of Man and Citizen.
      • They also brought the king back to Paris, ensuring that the increasingly militant Parisian crowd could keep watch on the royal family and prevent any counter- revolutionary coups.
      • Historian Peter McPhee argues that the revolution owed ‘its existence … once again to the armed intervention of the people of Paris’.

    Students can argue that ‘women received few benefits in the new regime’ by exploring how women were not considered full members of the body politic and suffered under the draconian legislation of the Terror.

    • Laws that defined citizenship were passed by the Assembly on 29 October and 22 December 1789. They were later enshrined in the Constitution, which was ratified by the king in September 1791.
    • Women were deemed ‘passive citizens’, meaning they could neither vote nor stand for public office in the new levels of government created by the Assembly.
    • McPhee: ‘The great majority of [male] politicians … were firmly opposed to women’s political rights.’
    • This perspective was typified by André Amar, a Jacobin and later member of the Committee of General Security, who argued that ‘women are unsuited for advanced thinking and serious reflection’.
    • Despite their exclusion from the lawmaking process, women were still subject to the law, including those related to the Terror.
    • This observation was made in the Declaration of the Rights of Women and Citizens, written by Olympe de Gouges in 1791. She was executed as a Girondin sympathiser on 3 November 1793.
    • Other notable victims of the Terror were Charlotte Corday, Marie Antoinette, Madam Roland and 16 Carmelite nuns who were executed on 17 July 1794 for refusing to abide by the Civil Constitution of the Clergy.
    • Overall, 9.3 per cent of victims of the Terror were women.

    Possible discussion points that qualify/challenge the view in the question Students can argue that ‘women received some benefits in the new regime’ by exploring how women could play an active, if unofficial, role in the politics of the new regime and secured some rights.

    • Some political clubs and societies were open to women, including the Society of Revolutionary Republican Citizenesses and the Société fraternelle des Minimes. Women were also welcome at the Cordeliers Club.
    • According to McPhee, around 40 women fought in the republican armies against France’s internal and external enemies.
    • Women also participated in journées, particularly when the price of food was the main issue. These included instances of ‘popular taxation’, in which women would pay what they considered a fair price for goods. This occurred in Paris in January 1792 and February 1793. Women were also prominent in the two journées of Germinal (April) and Prairial (May) of 1795.
    • Throughout the new regime, some pieces of legislation specifically benefitted women:
      • Inheritance laws introduced on 15 March 1790 and 8 April 1791 ensured that all children, not just the firstborn male child, could inherit an equal share of their parents’ estate.
      • On 20 September 1792, a divorce law was passed enabling marriages to be annulled on grounds of incompatibility. As either partner could initiate a divorce, this ‘challenged domestic relationships at a fundamental level’ (McPhee).

    Sample student response Considering the driving principles of the revolution, it is with some irony that historian William Doyle notes that ‘equality between men and women … was brushed aside as scarcely worthy of consideration’. It is certainly true that while women played a crucial role in the early foundation and consolidation of the revolution, they were not able to participate formally in the new political system that emerged from the ancien régime. Nevertheless, women were able to exert a de facto influence on the course of the revolution and secured some benefits, which were enshrined in law.

    Women played an important role in significant moments in the consolidation of the revolution. The narrative of the early course of the revolution was dominated by men, and only one woman, Marie Charpentier, was recognised by the National Assembly as a conqueror of the Bastille. However, women played a much more significant role in the October Days. On 5–6 October 1789, approximately 6000 working-class women from the market district of Paris marched to Versailles to present their grievances to the king and bring the royal family back to Paris. This was due to high bread prices and suspicions that the king was not sincere in his support for the revolution. The women stormed the Palace of Versailles and secured the king’s assent for the August Decrees and the Declaration of the Rights of Man and Citizen. They also brought the king back to Paris, ensuring that the increasingly militant Parisian crowd could keep a close watch on the royal family and prevent any counter-revolutionary coups.

    Despite their active role in safeguarding the revolution, women were not considered full members of the body politic and suffered under the draconian legislation of the Terror. Laws that defined citizenship were passed by the Assembly on 29 October and 22 December 1789 and were enshrined in the Constitution that was ratified by the king in September 1791. As a result, women were deemed ‘passive citizens’, meaning they could neither vote nor stand for public office in the new levels of government created by the Assembly. This was because ‘the great majority of [male] politicians … were firmly opposed to women’s political rights’ (McPhee). This perspective was typified by André Amar, Jacobin and later member of the Committee of General Security, who argued that ‘women are unsuited for advanced thinking and serious reflection’. Despite their exclusion from the lawmaking process, women were still subject to the law, including those related to the Terror. This observation was made in the Declaration of the Rights of Women and Citizens (1791), written by Olympe de Gouges, who was executed as a Girondin sympathiser on 3 November 1793. Other notable victims of the Terror were Charlotte Corday, Marie Antoinette and Madam Roland. Overall, 9.3 per cent of Terror victims were women.

    Nevertheless, women could play an active, if unofficial, role in the politics of the new regime and secured some rights. Some political clubs and societies were open to women, such as the Cordeliers Club and the Society of Revolutionary Republican Citizenesses. According to McPhee, some 40 women fought in the republican armies against France’s internal and external enemies. Women also participated in journées, particularly when the price of food was the main issue. These included instances of ‘popular taxation’, in which women would pay what they considered a fair price for goods. This occurred in Paris in January 1792 and February 1793. Women were also prominent in the final two journées of Germinal (April) and Prairial (May) of 1795. That said, some pieces of legislation introduced throughout the regime specifically benefitted women. Inheritance laws passed on 15 March 1790 and 8 April 1791 ensured that all children, not just the firstborn male child, could inherit an equal share of their parents’ estate. Further, on 20 September 1792, a divorce law was passed that enabled a marriage to be annulled on grounds of incompatibility. Either partner could initiate a divorce, and this ‘challenged domestic relationships at a fundamental level’ (McPhee).

    The underlying contradiction at the heart of the French Revolution was that a society partly founded on the principle of equality denied fundamental political rights to women. This was despite the role they had played in securing the revolution in October 1789. Nevertheless, while it is easy to dismiss women as passive observers or victims of the Terror, in reality they drove the course of the revolution and were able to secure for themselves some important social rights.

    Assessment criteria for Section B
    • Construction of a coherent and relevant historical argument that addresses the specific demands of the essay question
    • Demonstration of historical knowledge that is accurate and appropriate for the essay question
    • Application of historical thinking concepts such as cause and consequence, continuity and change, and/or historical significance
    • Use of sources as evidence to support a historical argument, including a range of primary sources, perspectives and historical interpretations
