    2026 Practice Exam — Revolutions

    American and French Revolution questions from the 2026 HTAV VCE History: Revolutions sample exam (Units 3 & 4), with the original sources. Your answers save in this browser.

    Section A — Short-answer questions with sources

    Question 1 (25 marks) · The American Revolution

    Read Sources 1–4 below, then answer parts a–e.

    Source 1

    A historical interpretation, published in 2000, of the consequences of the French and Indian War.

    The war … engendered1 new cultural tensions. Arrogant British officers treated American ‘provincials’ or ‘peasants’ (as they often called them) with contempt, which led to widespread suspicion of British policies. The war also increased the British national debt from £75 million to £133 million, setting off motions in Parliament that the prosperous2 colonists should shoulder part of this economic burden.

    Source: J Henretta and G Nobles, ‘Economics Drove the American Revolution’, in The American Revolution, K Werner (ed.), Greenhaven Press, California, 2000, pp. 29 and 30

    1. engendered – caused
    2. prosperous – successful in a financial sense
    Source 2

    An extract from the Declaration of the Causes and Necessity of Taking Up Arms, written by the Second Continental Congress and approved on 6 July 1775.

    But why should we enumerate1 our injuries in detail? By one statute it is declared that Parliament can ‘of right make laws to bind us IN ALL CASES WHATSOEVER’2. What is to defend us against so enormous, so unlimited a power? …

    We for ten years incessantly and ineffectually besieged the Throne as supplicants3. We reasoned, we remonstrated4 with Parliament in the most mild and decent language. But Administration5, sensible6 that we should regard these oppressive measures as freemen ought to do, sent over fleets and armies to enforce them. The indignation of the Americans was roused7, it is true; but it was the indignation of a virtuous, loyal, and affectionate people. A Congress of Delegates from the united colonies was assembled at Philadelphia on the fifth day of last September [1774]. We resolved again to offer [a] humble and dutiful petition to the King, and also addressed our fellow subjects of Great Britain. We have pursued every temperate, every respectful measure. …

    But subsequent events have shown how vain was this hope of finding moderation in our enemies. … Hostilities, thus commenced by the British troops, have been since prosecuted8 by them without regard to faith or reputation. …

    We are reduced to the alternative of choosing an unconditional submission to the tyranny of irritated ministers or resistance by force. The latter is our choice. We have counted the cost of this contest and find nothing so dreadful as voluntary slavery. Honor, justice, and humanity forbid us tamely to surrender that freedom which we received from our gallant9 ancestors, and which our innocent posterity10 have a right to receive from us.

    Source: Second Continental Congress, Declaration of the Causes and Necessity of Taking Up Arms, 6 July 1775; National Humanities Center, ‘Crisis: 1775: The Outbreak of War’, America in Class, 2013, <https://americainclass.org/sources/makingrevolution/crisis/text8/text8.htm>

    1. enumerate – count
    2. IN ALL CASES WHATSOEVER – refers to a phrase used in the Declaratory Act of 1766
    3. supplicants – a person who makes a humble plea to someone in power
    4. remonstrated – to make a forceful protest
    5. Administration – British Government
    6. sensible – aware
    7. roused – awoken
    8. prosecuted – continued
    9. gallant – brave
    10. posterity – descendants
    Source 3

    An engraving published in the Massachusetts Centinel on 16 January 1788. This image shows Massachusetts as the sixth state to ratify the Constitution.

    The text at the top reads, ‘States – like the gen’rous vine supported live, the strength they gain is from th’embrace they give THE FEDERAL PILLARS’.

    The text on the pillars read: DEL. (Delaware); PEN. (Pennsylvania); N. JER. (New Jersey); GEOR. (Georgia); CON. (Connecticut); MASS. (Massachusetts).

    The text at the bottom reads, ‘UNITED THEY STAND – DIVIDED FALL’.

    Source 4

    A historical interpretation, published in 1996, outlining the impact of the revolution on the role of women.

    How did the Revolution affect women? This is a difficult question to answer. The men who made the Revolution assumed that the war was theirs to make. There was no formal political context in which women might be consulted or might develop their collective judgment. But the war itself did speed the integration of women into the civil polity1. Whether a woman was whig or tory, her services in a largely guerrilla war were much sought after – as a provider of essential services for troops, as a civilian source of food and shelter, as a contributor of funds and supplies, as a spy. Women were challenged to commit themselves politically and then to justify their allegiance. The war raised once again the old question of whether a woman could be a patriot – that is, an essentially political person – and it also raised the question of what form female patriotism might take.

    These questions were not resolved by the war’s end. For example, one well-known element in British common law, which few Americans questioned, was coverture, the absorption of a married woman’s property into her husband’s control during the life of their marriage. Since only the citizen with independent control of property was thought to be able to exercise free will, it seemed to follow that the married woman had no independent political capacity. State legislatures in the new republic took care to show they understood that male and female political behavior required judgment by different standards. On the one hand women – married or unmarried – were responsible for acts of espionage or treason and were subject to the full penalties of the law. But except for overt acts of treason, the assumption still prevailed that married women could make no political choices of their own; for example, the wife of a tory was judged to be under such clear control of her husband that she perforce2 became a tory herself.

    Source: L Kerber, Women of the Republic: Intellect and Ideology in Revolutionary America, Norton, New York, 1986, p. 89

    1. polity – a politically organised society
    2. perforce – by necessity, or inevitably
    A2 MARKSIDENTIFY↩ Restored
    Identify two consequences of the French and Indian War as described in Source 1.
    0 words · aim for ~25
    HTAV 2025/2026 Guide to Responses — suggested discussion points and sample material, not the only acceptable answer.
    • The verb ‘identify’ indicates that students can simply select features of the source.
    • No explanation or analysis is required.
    • No facts from the student’s own knowledge are required.
    • Students should refer to the two features below.
    Suggested discussion points/sample student response
    • ‘Arrogant British officers treated American “provincials” or “peasants” … with contempt’, leading to ‘cultural tensions’.
    • Parliament believed that the ‘prosperous colonists should shoulder part of this economic burden’ from the war.
    B3 MARKSOUTLINE↩ Restored
    Outline the perspective given in Source 2 about why colonists were willing to take up arms against the British.
    0 words · aim for ~50
    HTAV 2025/2026 Guide to Responses — suggested discussion points and sample material, not the only acceptable answer.
    • The verb ‘outline’ indicates that students should give a high‑level overview or summary of the main ideas. This will work best with concise, full sentences.
    • The question asks for the ‘perspective’ given in Source 2. That is, students need to accurately summarise the overall opinion or viewpoint being presented by the document’s author.
    • There is no requirement for students to use their own knowledge. It is possible to achieve full marks using the source alone. However, some students may choose to draw on their own knowledge to contextualise or expand on ideas in the source.
    • As the question is worth 3 marks, it would be appropriate for students to provide three pieces of evidence from the source.
    Suggested discussion points
    • Colonists identified the actions of British administration as the clear reason for taking up arms.
    • They argued that they had been respectful using ‘mild and decent language’, but this only resulted in a show of military force, with ‘fleets and armies’ sent ‘to enforce’ laws.
    • Colonists suggested Britain started the hostilities and continued with them, regardless of their pleas.
    • They believed they had two choices: submit to British ‘tyranny’ or show ‘resistance by force’.
    • They believed they were gifted their freedom from their ‘gallant ancestors’ and had a right to maintain that freedom for future generations.

    Sample student response Colonists claimed that Parliament’s actions forced them to take up arms. Their respectful ‘remonstrances’ were answered with force, as Britain sent ‘fleets and armies to enforce’ (Source 2) the oppressive measures. Colonists asserted that they had only two choices: submit to ‘tyranny’ or show ‘resistance by force’ (S2). Ultimately, they did not wish to ‘surrender that freedom’ (S2) they believed was theirs.

    C5 MARKSEXPLAIN↩ Restored
    Using Source 2 and your own knowledge, explain how the actions of the Second Continental Congress contributed to a revolutionary situation up to 1776.
    0 words · aim for ~110
    HTAV 2025/2026 Guide to Responses — suggested discussion points and sample material, not the only acceptable answer.
    • The verb ‘explain’ indicates that students need to provide a structured and logical explanation that clarifies the relationship between concepts or ideas.
    • The question focuses on the Second Continental Congress, which is introduced towards the end of Area of Study 1. Therefore, responses should recognise that the importance of this group lay in the political arena, and that this body was responsible for making the final decision to seek independence. This question does not require students to make an argument; rather, knowledge should be used to explain causal links between actions of the Second Continental Congress and revolutionary tension.
    • To access the highest marks, students must make meaningful use of the source and incorporate other arguments backed by evidence from their own study.
    Suggested discussion points
    From the source
    • Source 2 is a key document produced by the Second Continental Congress. It justifies the colonies’ fight for independence by declaring their rights and listing the injustices they suffered under British rule.
    • The document highlights colonial frustrations that their ‘humble and dutiful petition’ was ignored, placing the blame for conflict on the British Parliament.
    • It stipulates that the colonies would rather choose ‘resistance by force’ than submit to the ‘tyranny of irritated ministers’.
    From own knowledge
    • The Second Continental Congress reconvened only one year after the First Continental Congress (May 1775).
    • Attendees included John Hancock, Samuel Adams, John Adams, Patrick Henry, Thomas Jefferson and George Washington.
    • By May 1775, the siege of Boston was underway, and so Congress oversaw the preparations for the war effort. They nominated George Washington as commander‑in‑chief of the new Continental Army and later approved the creation of the Continental Navy.
    • Congress issued new currency to finance the war effort.
    • Alongside the publication of the Declaration of the Causes and Necessities of Taking Up Arms (Source 2), Congress also drafted and adopted the Olive Branch Petition (July 1775) as one final attempt to seek a peaceful solution to the brewing conflict.
    • By 1776, the Continental Congress drafted, then adopted, the Declaration of Independence (adopted 4 July 1776).
    • They remained as the governing body for the newly formed United States of America as they embarked on the War of Independence.

    Sample student response The Second Continental Congress (convened May 1775) turned colonial resistance into a coordinated bid for independence. Source 2 highlights the consequence of Britain using troops against colonists, resulting in ‘resistance by force’ rather than colonial submission to the ‘tyranny of irritated ministers’. After fighting erupted at Lexington and Concord (April 1775), the Second Continental Congress assumed the powers of a national government, creating the Continental Army with George Washington as its commander. They also sought to finance this army, issued paper currency, and organised attempts to secure foreign support, notably from France. Although Congress sought peace with the Olive Branch Petition (July 1775), they ‘counted the cost of this contest’ (S2) and in early 1776 encouraged states to form new republican governments. They also commissioned a committee to draft a Declaration of Independence, adopted on 4 July 1776. In this way, Congress provided an alternate political authority, leading directly to coordinated armed resistance against the British.

    D9 MARKSEVALUATE↩ Restored
    Evaluate the significance of the ratification of the Constitution in consolidating the authority of the revolutionary government by 1789. In your response, refer to Source 3 and your own knowledge.
    0 words · aim for ~220
    HTAV 2025/2026 Guide to Responses — suggested discussion points and sample material, not the only acceptable answer.
    • The command term for this question is ‘evaluate’. This means that students should aim to form a judgement.
    • The question asks students to consider the significance (importance) of the ratification of the Constitution in consolidating authority (i.e., winning support, overcoming opposition, and establishing an effective government).
    • Strong responses will identify challenges confronting the revolutionary government (e.g., political divisions between Federalists and Anti‑Federalists, fears of centralised power, concerns over diminished state sovereignty) and then analyse how ratification provided the means or opportunity to respond to these challenges (e.g., the Federalist Papers shaping public opinion, the promise of a Bill of Rights as a compromise, the prestige of Washington lending legitimacy to the new framework).
    • Students may also choose to contend that ratification was significant, but that other developments were also equally important in consolidating authority. For example, a student might argue that Washington’s status, reputation and leadership were just as important, as his personal endorsement of the new framework countered opposition and gave it a legitimacy that ratification alone could not guarantee. In this case, students should begin by exploring the significance of ratification before pivoting to their additional or concessional argument later in the response.
    • Note that a counter or concessional argument is not required to score highly. A sustained, well‑supported judgement arguing in a single direction can be equally effective, provided it demonstrates genuine evaluation rather than description.
    Suggested discussion points
    From the source
    • The source asserts that the states would be strengthened by uniting under the federal structure. This is represented by the pillars for each state (DEL represents Delaware, PEN represents Pennsylvania, etc.) being linked by the stars above them and the hand of God lifting them into place.
    • ‘United they stand, divided [they] fall’ issues a warning that the future of the country may be in danger if the states do not unite under the federal structure.
    From own knowledge
    • Calls to create a constitution with a stronger executive and nationwide powers were raised after the War of Independence. Criticisms of the Articles of Confederation highlighted the ineffectiveness of the Confederation Congress to enforce laws, raise revenue and regulate the competing interests of each state.
    • The makers of the Constitution included a clause allowing for only nine of 13 ratifying states to be required for its approval. This alarmed many who assumed a unanimous agreement would be needed.
    • The process of accepting or ratifying the Constitution proved contentious. Many states were reluctant to yield some of their authority and began questioning the levels of power given to the new national government.
    • The Federalist Debates were pivotal in swaying public opinion and showed that many people still did not trust powerful governments. Between October 1787 and May 1788, Alexander Hamilton, John Jay and James Madison wrote the Federalist Papers, in which they argued for the ratification of the Constitution. Anti‑Federalist concerns also led to calls for a Bill of Rights to protect individual liberties against the strong national government. Anti‑Federalists included Patrick Henry, George Mason and Samuel Adams.
    • The Constitution was approved by the ninth state New Hampshire on 21 June 1788. This ratification made the Constitution effective, officially ending the government under the Articles of Confederation.
    • George Washington gave his support to the Constitution. As president of the Constitutional Convention, his endorsement reassured uncertain states that the new government would be stable and trustworthy, while also encouraging wavering delegates and citizens to unite behind the proposed federal framework. Washington would serve as the first president.
    Historical perspectives
    • George Washington (1786): ‘Thirteen Sovereignties pulling against each other, and all tugging at the federal head, will soon bring ruin to the whole.’
    • Thomas Jefferson (1787): ‘A bill of rights is what the people are entitled to against every government on earth, general or particular, and what no just government should refuse, or rest on interference.’
    • Alexander Hamilton (1788): ‘A nation, without a national government, is, in my view, an awful spectacle’ (Federalist No. 85).
    Historical interpretations
    • Gordon S. Wood (on the Constitution): ‘It was without doubt a monumental political act, but it did not solve many of the political problems its creators expected it to solve.’
    • Robert Middlekauff: ‘Opposition to the Constitution should not have surprised anyone. The Revolution after all had been fought over questions of governance and rights.’
    • Howard Zinn suggests that the new Bill of Rights was created merely to make the Constitution ‘more acceptable to the public’, asserting it was ‘perfectly designed to build popular backing for the new government’.
    • Alan Taylor: ‘[Federalists] created a useful fiction: that a united, homogeneous, and sovereign American people created the Constitution. Hence, the document begins with “We the People” rather than “We the States”.’
    • Joseph J. Ellis: ‘No less a figure than Washington fervently believed that the failure to create a sovereign national government would represent a repudiation of everything he had fought for.’

    Sample student response The ratification of the Constitution throughout 1787 to 1788 was highly significant in establishing a stable national framework but was not sufficient on its own to secure the authority of the new revolutionary government. To achieve this, the persuasive arguments of the Federalists as well as the endorsement of George Washington were needed to convince the broader public to accept the new federal authority.

    Source 3 asserts that the states would be strengthened by uniting under the federal structure, created to replace the Articles of Confederation (ratified March 1781). In the image, each state’s pillar is linked to the previous, conveying a sense of strength and solidarity. This implies the new Constitution’s strengthened powers to enforce laws, raise much needed revenue (Article I, Section 8) and regulate interstate issues (Articles II, III). Concerns about instability, demonstrated during Shays’ Rebellion (1786 to 1787), is also reflected in Source 3, where the warning ‘United they stand, divided [they] fall’ highlights that the country’s future may be in danger if the states do not ratify. However, ratification was contested by leaders like Patrick Henry, concerned that their newly won individual liberties would be threatened under such a powerful government. Robert Middlekauff highlights that the revolution ‘had been fought over questions of governance and rights’ and that the opposition from Anti‑Federalists continued those same protests. The Federalist Debates (1787 to 1788) saw leaders like Alexander Hamilton and James Madison persuade their countrymen that the Constitution was an extension of the revolutionary ideals fought for, not a betrayal of them. Based on Anti‑Federalist concerns, Madison then drafted the Bill of Rights (adopted in 1791) with the promised amendments that ensured support for the new Constitution. In addition, George Washington lent his considerable reputation to approving the new framework, overseeing its creation as president of the Constitutional Convention (1787). He later nominated as the first president to oversee its implementation. Much support for the Constitution came from the belief that it would work because Washington would lead it. As such, ratification of the Constitution was essential in establishing the new political framework, but securing it depended on its defence offered in the Federalist Debates and the symbolic support of Washington.

    E6 MARKSANALYSE↩ Restored
    Using Source 4 and your own knowledge, analyse one continuity and one change in the experiences of women by 1789.
    0 words · aim for ~140
    HTAV 2025/2026 Guide to Responses — suggested discussion points and sample material, not the only acceptable answer.
    • The verb ‘analyse’ indicates that students should break down this question into parts and explain each part separately.
    • The question specifically requires students to focus on a single aspect of continuity and a single aspect of change. If additional or multiple aspects of continuity and/or change are included, they should be ignored when marking.
    • A continuity is any instance where conditions either remained largely the same throughout, or where changes were short‑lived and there was a reversion to the status quo.
      • To demonstrate continuity, students must establish that conditions at the end of the revolution were similar to those when the revolutionary government assumed power.
    • A change refers to any condition where the situation afterwards is clearly and significantly different to conditions beforehand.
      • To demonstrate change, students must establish that conditions at the end of the revolutionary period were substantially different from those when the revolutionary government assumed power.
    • The strongest responses will offer comparisons between two points in time to establish whether or not change occurred.
      • Since no date range is provided for this question, students may optionally choose to draw on evidence from Area of Study 1 (1754 to 4 July 1776) to establish what life was like before the revolution. However, there is no obligation for students to do this. They can still achieve full marks by giving a well‑rounded discussion focused entirely on the period 4 July 1776 to 1789 which corresponds with Area of Study 2.
    • To access the highest marks, students must make skillful use of evidence from both the source and their own knowledge.
    Suggested discussion points
    From the source
    • Kerber recognises that there was ‘no formal political context’ for women in either the pre‑revolutionary society or the new society.
    • She suggests there was a limited increase in political agency during the war, though it ‘did speed the integration of women into the civil polity’, as their services in the war ‘were much sought after’.
    • She highlights how the law of coverture was a consistent presence, and that this was used at the time to suggest that ‘the married woman had no independent political capacity’.
    • Kerber suggests that ‘the wife of a Tory was judged to be under … clear control of her husband’ which automatically made her a Tory by association, indicating the inability of women to act according to their own beliefs.
    • Overall, Kerber asserts that little change occurred for women as a result of the revolution: ‘Except for overt acts of treason, the assumption still prevailed that married women could make no political choices of their own.’
    From own knowledge Prior to the revolution
    • Women had no independent legal or political identity. Daughters belonged to their fathers in a legal sense, and married women’s property and wages belonged to their husbands under the law of coverture.
    • Women could not vote, hold office or formally participate in political debate.
    • Social expectations saw women as an extension of the household to which they belonged. This placed women firmly in the domestic sphere, where their value was in managing the household and in raising children.
    • Women did use their domestic influence for political purposes (e.g., the boycotts and spinning parties held by the Daughters of Liberty). These female Patriot groups became symbols of resistance.
    Continuities – After the revolution
    • Neither the Articles of Confederation nor the Constitution granted women voting rights or the ability to hold office. Citizenship in the new society was framed around male participation.
    • Coverture remained intact – though New Jersey did briefly allow some women who owned property to vote after 1776. At this time, most states used terms such as ‘free male citizens’ in state constitutions.
    Changes – During the War of Independence
    • With the absence of men fighting the war, many women managed farms, shops and finances, increasing their independence and leadership in these areas.
    • While some tried to participate in direct combat (e.g., Deborah Sampson), these were few in number and did not represent the broader female experience. Most women who followed the Continental Army were ‘camp followers’ (wives who followed their husbands out of financial necessity). They took on low‑paid jobs such as laundry and nursing the sick men.
    • Loyalist women faced significant hardship during the War of Independence, with many having their property seized and being socially ostracised.
    Changes – After the revolution
    • There were very limited changes for women after the revolution. Calls for ‘liberty’ and ‘natural rights’ during the revolution encouraged many to consider the role women played in society. Notably, Abigail Adams (John Adams’s wife) requested the founders to ‘remember the ladies and be more generous and favourable to them’ (1776). Her husband, however, dismissed this as a joke.
    • Women’s roles as mothers expected to raise patriotic sons highlighted the importance of education for girls.

    Sample student response Although women exercised greater political agency in the years prior to and during the War of Independence (1776 to 1783), the political framework of the new society remained the exclusive domain of men. Source 4 identifies that there was ‘no formal political context’ for women’s participation prior to 1776. However, Kerber suggests that the war helped ‘speed the integration of women into the civil polity’ and brought them new opportunities to play an active political role. She identifies the important roles women played in supporting the Continental Army, serving as camp followers providing ‘essential services for troops’ (S4) or raising funds through organised committees such as the Daughters of Liberty. Such roles granted an increased, although short‑lived, sense of political agency for women. However, after the War of Independence, women continued to be excluded from voting or office‑holding, owing to the belief that ‘married [women] had no independent political capacity’ (S4). Neither the Articles of Confederation (ratified 1781) nor the Constitution (ratified 1788) granted women political suffrage, as citizenship in the new society was framed around male participation.

    Question 2 (25 marks) · The French Revolution

    Read Sources 5–8 below, then answer parts a–e.

    Source 5

    A historical interpretation, published in 1959, of the pressures from both the royal household and popular movements in challenging King Louis XVI’s absolute authority in June 1789.

    To force the pace and overawe1 Paris, foreign troops were being concentrated on the outskirts of the city: on 3 June already … German and Hungarian regiments [were] brought in on the pretext of preventing a renewed outburst of rioting in the Faubourg Saint-Antoine. The intentions of the Court Party2, grouped around Marie-Antoinette and the king’s younger brother, the Comte d’Artois, were becoming clear: on the night of 22 June [1789] the king was persuaded to dismiss Necker and to overawe the National Assembly by a display of military force. The plot miscarried3: thousands invaded the courtyard of the palace to demand that Necker be retained in office; soldiers under the command of the Prince de Conti refused to obey the command to fire; and the deputies, rallied by Mirabeau in an historic speech, refused to disperse. The king was compelled to yield4.

    Source: G Rudé, The Crowd in the French Revolution, Oxford University Press, Oxford, 1959, p. 47

    1. overawe – to impress (someone or a group) so much that they are silent or unable to act
    2. Court Party – the group of courtiers and royals typically present in the royal household
    3. miscarried – failed to attain the intended outcome
    4. yield – give way to arguments, demands or pressure
    Source 6

    An excerpt from Charles Alexandre de Calonne’s speech to the Assembly of Notables on 22 February 1787, in which he criticised the system of privilege and proposed changes to France’s tax system.

    Abuses [in tax payment] are defended by self-interest, influence, wealth and ancient prejudices which seem to be hallowed1 by time; but what are all these together compared with the common good and the necessity of the state? These abuses oppress the wealth-producing, laboring class: the abuses of pecuniary2 privilege; exceptions to the general rule; and so many unjust exemptions which only relieve one section of taxpayers by aggravating the condition of the others. …

    The projects which the King intends to impart to you [are] plans for the public good long contemplated by experienced statesmen and by the government itself. Some have been attempted in part and all seem to have the backing of the nation, but hitherto3 their complete implementation appeared impracticable4 because of the difficulty of reconciling a host of local customs, claims, privileges and conflicting interests.

    Source: J Flammermont, Remontrances du Parlement de Paris au XVIIIe siècle: Vol 1, Imprimerie Nationale, Paris, 1888–1898, pp. 189–198

    1. hallowed – greatly revered and honoured
    2. pecuniary – relating to money
    3. hitherto – until now
    4. impracticable – impossible to do in practice
    Source 7

    A political cartoon, titled Le déménagement du clergé (The Removal of the Clergy) and published in 1790, showing parish priests leaving a church after the National Assembly’s decree of biens nationaux, which nationalised Church property.

    The text at the top reads, Nous allons à la grace de Dieu (We are going to the grace of God).

    The first line of text at the bottom reads, Le Demenagement du Clergé (The Removal of the Clergy).

    The second line of text reads, J’ai perdu mes bénéfices, rien n’égale ma douleur (I have lost my privileges, nothing equals my sorrow).

    Source 8

    A historical interpretation, published in 1965, of the bourgeoisie’s influence and the political divisions within the National Convention after its establishment on 20 September 1792.

    The people’s revolution of 10 August1 and the war against Prussia and Austria had brought a temporary halt to the great advance of the bourgeoisie. … With the demise of the Feuillants, the intellectual élites of eighteenth-century Enlightenment had vanished from the political scene, leaving in their place men who owed everything to circumstance and who were to find themselves taking on responsibilities for which neither their educational background nor their political experience fitted them. For almost a whole year, French politics were to be dominated by two factions. The Jacobin democrats of Paris, who had established the revolutionary Commune of 10 August, sat high up at the back of the National Convention and thus came to be known as the ‘Mountain’. These ‘Montagnards’ were a minority group, and for a long time the sympathies of the bourgeoisie were with their opponents, known at the time as the Brissotins, or Girondins. …

    At first, however, the distinction between Girondins and Montagnards was not at all clear-cut. Socially, both factions belonged largely to the middle bourgeoisie2; politically, they were both committed to the democratic movement; intellectually, there were nearly all equally contemptuous3 of religion and its priests (in this respect, Robespierre was not typical of the Montagnards). Both factions were small in numbers, but by a combination of various forces – party spirit, ministerial solidarity and pure chance – they were soon to find themselves bitterly opposed in a mighty political struggle.

    Source: F Furet and D Richet, La révolution, S Hardman (trans.), Librairie Hachette et Société d’Études et de Publications Économiques, Paris, 1965, p. 147

    1. The people’s revolution of 10 August – the storming of the Tuileries Palace
    2. middle bourgeoisie – middle-ranking members of the bourgeoisie, typically professionals, senior managers, and established business owners
    3. contemptuous – feeling that a person or thing is worthless or beneath consideration
    A2 MARKSIDENTIFY↩ Restored
    Using Source 5, identify two reasons why the king was forced to yield his authority on the night of 22 June 1789.
    0 words · aim for ~25
    HTAV 2025/2026 Guide to Responses — suggested discussion points and sample material, not the only acceptable answer.
    • The verb ‘identify’ indicates that students can simply select features of the source.
    • No explanation or analysis is required.
    • No facts from the student’s own knowledge are required.
    • Students could refer to any two of the features below.
    Suggested discussion points/sample student response
    • ‘Thousands [of protesters] invaded the courtyard of the palace.’
    • Royal soldiers ‘refused to obey the command to fire’ given by their superior officer.
    • The deputies of the National Assembly ‘refused to disperse’.
    B3 MARKSOUTLINE↩ Restored
    Using Source 6, outline Calonne’s perspective on fiscal privileges in the old regime.
    0 words · aim for ~50
    HTAV 2025/2026 Guide to Responses — suggested discussion points and sample material, not the only acceptable answer.
    • The verb ‘outline’ indicates that students should give a high‑level overview or summary of the main ideas. This will work best with concise, full sentences.
    • The question asks for the ‘perspective’ given in Source 6. That is, students need to accurately summarise the overall opinion or viewpoint being presented by Calonne.
    • There is no requirement for students to use their own knowledge. It is possible to achieve full marks using the source alone. However, some students may choose to draw on their own knowledge to contextualise or expand on ideas in the source.
    • As the question is worth 3 marks, it would be appropriate for students to provide three pieces of evidence from the source.
    Suggested discussion points
    • Multiple factors combined to defend abuses in tax payment, including ‘self‑interest, influence, wealth and ancient prejudices’.
    • ‘The common good and the necessity of the state’ should be more important than defending abuses of the tax system.
    • Abuses in tax payments oppressed the ‘wealth‑producing, laboring class’.
    • ‘Unjust exemptions’ on various taxes ‘[relieved] one section of taxpayers’ (typically the First and Second Estates) ‘by aggravating the condition of the others’ (the Third Estate).

    Sample student response Calonne asserts that weakness in the tax system was due to a combination of abuses, including ‘self‑interest, wealth and ancient prejudices’ (Source 6). However, he also believed that the ‘common good and the necessity of the state’ should take priority over abuses of the tax system – typically by members of the First and Second Estates – which oppressed the ‘wealth‑producing, laboring’ (S6) classes. While unjust exemptions relieved the nobles and clergy of most taxes, these only ‘aggravated the condition’ of the Third Estate.

    C5 MARKSEXPLAIN↩ Restored
    Using Source 6 and your own knowledge, explain how failure to reform the economy contributed to a revolutionary situation by July 1789.
    0 words · aim for ~110
    HTAV 2025/2026 Guide to Responses — suggested discussion points and sample material, not the only acceptable answer.
    • The verb ‘explain’ indicates that students need to provide a structured and logical explanation that clarifies the relationship between concepts or ideas.
    • The question focuses on failures to reform the French economy by July 1789. Therefore, responses should demonstrate knowledge of multiple attempts at reform, notably through finance ministers Turgot, Necker, Calonne and Brienne
      • though other knowledge may also be used. This question does not require

    students to make an argument; rather, knowledge should be used to explain causal links from failed reforms to economic pressure and revolutionary tension.

    • To access the highest marks, students must make meaningful use of the source and incorporate other arguments backed by evidence from their own study.
    Suggested discussion points
    From the source
    • The Third Estate was oppressed by the First and Second Estates’ unequal access to fiscal privileges.
    • The First and Second Estates openly defended those abuses in pursuit of their own self‑interest.
    • They perpetuated abuses in tax payment by using their influence and wealth and by exploiting ancient prejudices against the Third Estate.
    • High‑quality practical reforms proposed by the king appear to have been blocked by ‘conflicting interests’ among the First and Second Estates.
    From own knowledge
    • Failure to institute structural reform meant escalating debt from loans funding the American War of Independence could never be effectively paid off.
    • Without reforms on wealth distribution and structures such as the tax system, France’s economy could not withstand the pressure of unpredictable events like the harsh winter of 1788.
    • Successive finance ministers had no solid foundation upon which to do their job. People such as Calonne and Brienne were constantly forced to adapt and reshape reforms with little continuity.

    Sample student response France’s economy was riddled with structural weaknesses, making it unfit to withstand the pressure of several crises leading up to July 1789. Chief among these was its unequal and unreliable revenue stream, which relied on a taxation system hindered by ‘pecuniary privilege … exceptions to the general rule [and] many unjust exemptions’ (Source 6). Not only did this aggravate the condition of the wealth‑producing Third Estate, it also kept 23 million peasants in subsistence, hampering their capacity to combat crises like the drought and harsh winter of 1788. This generated mass food shortages and caused inflation in the late 1780s, with the price of bread rising from nine sous to 15 in 1789 alone. These crises could have been alleviated by purposeful, targeted and consistent reforms, but the lack of time and trust given to finance ministers from Turgot to Jacques Necker meant major programs by Calonne (1787) or Brienne (1788) never had the opportunity to make a lasting impact.

    D9 MARKSEVALUATE↩ Restored
    Evaluate the significance of challenging the Church in consolidating the new regime’s power. In your response, refer to Source 7 and your own knowledge.
    0 words · aim for ~220
    HTAV 2025/2026 Guide to Responses — suggested discussion points and sample material, not the only acceptable answer.
    • The command term for this question is ‘evaluate’. This means that students should aim to form a judgement.
    • The question asks students to consider the significance (importance) of challenges to the Church in consolidating authority (i.e., winning support, overcoming opposition, and establishing an effective government).
    • Students should demonstrate an understanding of both key components – what challenging the Church involved (e.g., the biens nationaux, the Civil Constitution of the Clergy, the Clerical Oath) and what consolidating the new regime’s power meant in practice (e.g., establishing the National Assembly’s supremacy, repositioning the king, securing popular legitimacy through the August Decrees and the Declaration of the Rights of Man and Citizen [DORMAC]). Then, they must analyse the relationship between them.
    • Students may also contend that challenging the Church was not as significant as other developments. In this case, students should begin by exploring the significance of challenging the Church before pivoting to their counterargument later in the response.
    • Note that a counterargument is not required to score highly. A sustained, well‑supported judgement arguing in a single direction can be equally effective, provided it demonstrates genuine evaluation rather than description.
    Suggested discussion points
    From the source
    • The title Le déménagement du clergé (The Removal of the Clergy) shows direct state action against the Church, symbolised by the priests exiting the church building.
    • The text Nous allons à la grace de Dieu (We are going to the grace of God) suggests that the Church became powerless and newly dependent on the National Assembly, with faith as their only comfort.
    • The text J’ai perdu mes bénéfices, rien n’égale ma douleur (I have lost my privileges, nothing equals my sorrow) shows loss of privileges due to the August Decrees (5 to 11 August 1789) and the nationalisation of Church lands, demonstrating the removal of a major rival source of authority and the National Assembly’s supremacy over traditional institutions.
    From own knowledge
    • Challenges to the Church:
      • The biens nationaux (2 November 1789) challenged the Church’s sovereignty in terms of property ownership, while also drastically reducing its capacity to perform its duties.
      • The National Assembly’s rationalisation of administration (e.g., involving a reduction to 44,000 local communes) decreased the number of postings available for a range of clergy, from bishops all the way down to parish priests.
      • The Civil Constitution of the Clergy (12 July 1790) confronted priests with recognising the authority of the state over the Pope (and by extension, God) – directly contradicting their spiritual custom.
      • The Clerical Oath (27 November 1790) forced priests to openly defy the Church in favour of the state, or else they would suffer consequences from the National Assembly.
    • New regime’s power:
      • The National Assembly’s power was contingent on how it positioned the king in the new society. This can be explored through the Vote on the Powers of the King (10 September 1789) and the Fundamental Principles of Government (1 October 1789).
      • The National Assembly was interested in cementing itself as national representatives through a set of sweeping new reforms, including the August Decrees (5 to 11 August 1789) and the DORMAC (26 August 1789).

    Sample student response For the National Assembly, consolidating power in a new regime required denying not only the old regime’s monarchical supremacy but also the Church’s institutional supremacy. Given the National Assembly’s desire to channel power back into state rather than papal apparatuses, it is unsurprising that it began with taking down the Church. This is represented in the painting The Removal of the Clergy (Source 7), which shows a group of clergymen exiting a church building following the decree of biens nationaux. The Assembly’s desire to consolidate power echoes the nationalistic language of the Abbé Sièyes’s What Is the Third Estate? (January 1789), which proclaimed the value of fraternity in nationhood. After all, Sièyes attended the Tennis Court Oath (20 June) that year, where it was declared ‘never to separate … until the constitution of the realm is drawn up and fixed upon solid foundations’. Thus, the Assembly’s early reforms made quick work of establishing itself as the legitimate ruling power in the state. Its August Decrees (5 to 11) aimed at further disempowering the privileged orders, depicted in Source 7 through the declaration, ‘I have lost my privileges, nothing equals my sorrow’. Its Vote on the Powers of the King (10 September 1789) – where a suspensive veto was conceded – made way for

    the subsequent declaration of power in the Fundamental Principles of Government (1 October 1789). But the Catholic institution remained a potential rival to the new regime’s order. The Assembly initially sought to legitimise power by advancing state superiority through the Civil Constitution of the Clergy (12 July 1790). However, when opposition to this was clear (through counters made in the Assembly by 30 clergymen on 30 October 1790) and yet unenforceable, the Assembly forced the clergy to take the Clerical Oath (27 November 1790) and publicly declare support for the nation or face punishment, like defunding or even deportation (though the latter was vetoed by the king in December 1791). Though challenging the Church significantly ruptured France’s stability (McPhee), it was a clear and purposeful strategy by the National Assembly to consolidate its power in line with previous attempts to disempower the great institutions of the old regime.

    E6 MARKSANALYSE↩ Restored
    Using Source 8 and your own knowledge, analyse one continuity and one change in the bourgeoisie’s influence by 1795.
    0 words · aim for ~140
    HTAV 2025/2026 Guide to Responses — suggested discussion points and sample material, not the only acceptable answer.
    • The verb ‘analyse’ indicates that students should break down this question into parts and explain each part separately.
    • The question specifically requires students to focus on a single aspect of continuity and a single aspect of change. If additional or multiple aspects of continuity and/or change are included, they should be ignored when marking.
    • A continuity is any instance where conditions either remained largely the same throughout, or where changes were short‑lived and there was a reversion to the status quo.
      • To demonstrate continuity, students must establish that conditions at the end of the revolution were similar to those when the revolutionary government assumed power.
    • A change refers to any condition where the situation afterwards is clearly and significantly different to conditions beforehand.
      • To demonstrate change, students must establish that conditions at the end of the revolutionary period were substantially different from those when the revolutionary government assumed power.
    • The strongest responses will offer comparisons between two points in time to establish whether or not change occurred.
      • Since no date range is provided for this question, students may optionally choose to draw on evidence from Area of Study 1 (1774 to 4 August 1789) to establish what life was like before the revolution. However, there is no obligation for students to do this. They can still achieve full marks by giving a well‑rounded discussion focused entirely on the period 5 August 1789 to 1795 which corresponds with Area of Study 2.
    • To access the highest marks, students must make skillful use of evidence from both the source and their own knowledge.
    Suggested discussion points
    From the source
    • Evidence that illustrates change:
      • The largely bourgeois intelligentsia, represented by the Feuillants, declined in influence and consequently ‘vanished from the political scene’.
    • Evidence that illustrates continuity:
      • The bourgeoisie had already secured strong representation in both the National and Legislative assemblies between 1789 and 1792. This continued under the popularly elected National Convention, which ‘belonged largely to the middle bourgeoisie’, nominally divided between the Jacobins and the Girondins.
    From own knowledge Changes
    • Compared to the nobility and monarchy, the bourgeoisie’s power grew rapidly from early 1789 through the rule of successive assemblies, as they secured greater representation and influence.
    • The 1791 Constitution accentuated bourgeois power, as many were able to take advantage of qualifying as ‘active citizens’.
    • The promotion of meritocracy (e.g., as in the DORMAC) benefited educated bourgeois men. However, at the same time, the reduction in venal offices could cost wealthy but otherwise untalented bourgeoisie their postings.
    • Wealthy bourgeoisie were able to purchase previously unavailable land thanks to movements such as the biens nationaux and the increasing number of émigrés.
    • Moves towards economic liberalism, such as reducing trade barriers across markets within France, aligned closely with bourgeois interests in generating wealth.
    • The bourgeoisie established themselves as a new dominant social elite.
    Continuities
    • Ultimately, the bourgeoisie remained wealthy throughout this period, continuing to control the flow of commerce within France.
    • The bourgeoisie also remained socially superior to peasants and urban workers.
    • There was little change in the relationship between the bourgeoisie and the poorer disenfranchised members of the Third Estate.

    Sample student response Bourgeoisie influence accelerated rapidly between 1774 and 1795. In the late ancien regime, they lacked authentic political representation outside special assemblies such as the Assembly of Notables (February to May 1787) or the Estates‑General. This changed with the rapid declaration of the National Assembly in June 1789, through to their swearing of the Tennis Court Oath and into the second half of the year, when sweeping decrees were manufactured to serve bourgeois interests. The DORMAC’s (26 August 1789) focus on men being ‘free and equal’ discouraged alienation from the nobility, while business and civic interests were protected through legislation such as the Le Chapelier Law (14 June 1791) and the 1791 Constitution respectively. This change helped consolidate several continuities, primarily the bourgeoisie’s maintenance of representation between all major assemblies including the National Assembly, the Legislative Assembly and the National Convention – which even by 1792 still ‘belonged largely to the middle bourgeoisie’ (Source 8). From the DORMAC, which protected their property rights as ‘inviolable’ (instead targeting privileges of the First and Second Estates) to their capitalisation of additional properties after the biens nationaux (2 November 1789), the bourgeoisie were typically in power to preserve their wealth.

    Section B — Essay

    Write an essay on one of the following. The 20-mark essay is assessed against the criteria below.

    Question 1 (20 marks) · The American Revolution
    ESSAY20 MARKS↩ Restored
    ‘The rise of organised Patriot groups was pivotal in causing the revolution because their actions heightened colonial unrest and generated the momentum needed to break from Britain.’

    To what extent do you agree? Use evidence to support your response.
    0 words · aim for ~700
    HTAV 2025/2026 Guide to Responses — suggested discussion points and sample material, not the only acceptable answer.
    General advice
    • This prompt draws on knowledge from Area of Study 1 only. Students will not be rewarded marks for evidence they include from Area of Study 2.
    • To achieve high marks, it is recommended that students follow this essay structure:
      • Introduction that clearly states their contention and outlines their main arguments
      • At least three body paragraphs, each clearly focused on one argument
      • A brief conclusion, restating the extent to which they agreed with the view in the essay prompt
    • The prompt contains three ideas students need to evaluate:
      • Whether or not the rise of organised Patriot groups heightened colonial unrest and/or generated the momentum needed to break from Britain
      • Whether or not the consequences of their actions were pivotal in causing the revolution
      • Whether or not the impact of organised Patriot groups were more, equally or less significant than other factors in causing the revolution
    • Students can approach this question by:
      • agreeing fully with the view – finding several ways in which the viewpoint can be considered true
      • agreeing to some extent – supporting some aspects of the view while challenging others
      • disagreeing fully with the view – arguing that the Patriot groups were not pivotal and that other causes were more significant.
    • In Section B, to achieve the highest possible marks, students must effectively use historical interpretations in their response.
    Suggested discussion points
    • Key details students could consider when planning their response include:
      • Who were the different Patriot groups?
      • What did the actions of these Patriot groups lead to? Did they generate the ‘momentum needed to break from Britain’? If so, then how? If not, who or what else did?
      • The prompt suggests their ‘rise was pivotal’. Consider what the word rise implies and whether their actions were pivotal. Were they the most important cause of revolution, or were there other causes, either equal in weighting or more significant?
      • The prompt also suggests their actions led to social unrest and generating ‘momentum’. Students should consider if this was the only way that Patriot groups contributed towards the revolution, and could also suggest other ways they contributed, such as through political actions.

    Patriot groups Students should recognise that there were a range of organised Patriot groups that formed in the years prior to 1776:

    • Sons of Liberty (from 1765): This group formed initially in Massachusetts during the Stamp Act (1765) crisis to resist British taxation and imperial authority. They transformed opposition to British taxation into organised public resistance.
    • Daughters of Liberty (from 1765): This was a women’s movement supporting boycotts and economic resistance. Their widespread economic boycotts and homespun campaigns extended resistance into daily life.
    • Committees of Correspondence (from 1772): This network of local groups shared information and coordinated responses to British policies. They created an intercolonial communication network that unified political responses.
    • Committees of Safety (from 1774): Formed as a response to the Coercive Acts (1774), these committees enforced the boycotts against the British. They monitored loyalty to the cause and assumed local governing powers, effectively weakening British authority at the community level.
    • Provincial Congresses (1774 to 1776): These extra‑legal Patriot assemblies formed when royal governors dissolved colonial assemblies, notably after the Massachusetts Government Act (May 1774). They acted as de facto Patriot governments, organising militias and preparing colonies for armed resistance.
    • Local Patriot militias and minutemen (1774 to 1775): These were community‑based armed groups who prepared to fight British troops. Their actions led to shots fired at Lexington and Concord (April 1775). These groups demonstrated that colonists were ready to defend their newly asserted rights.
    • The Continental Congress (1774 to 1776): This was an intercolonial body that eventually coordinated political, economic and military resistance. It ultimately declared independence from Britain.
    Evidence to support the view given in the question
    • The different Patriot groups mobilised broad sections of colonial society. Through public protests, community boycotts, homespun campaigns, and militia mobilisation, Patriot groups involved men, women, merchants, labourers and farmers, and so they pulled a broad number of ordinary people into active resistance, increasing the number of people opposing British authority.
    • They also increased the strategic coordination of the colonies, turning anger into organised campaigns, protests and boycotts. For example, Committees of Correspondence ensured that if one colony protested a British Act, others would follow.
    • They displaced British authority by creating alternative systems of governance. This erosion of British power meant the colonies were effectively self‑governing before independence was declared.
    Evidence to challenge or qualify the view given in the question
    • Patriot groups formed as a direct response to British attempts to tighten their control. The end of salutary neglect and British tax revenue Acts were themselves key to generating colonial anger, as they directly challenged colonial expectations of self‑government.
    • The change in British policy, seen through the punitive Coercive Acts, was regarded as a direct assault on colonial rights, driving a clear wedge between the British and the colonists. These Acts led directly to the formation of some Patriot groups, such as the Continental Congress.
    • Military confrontations escalated tensions to the point where compromises appeared unachievable. The battles of Lexington and Concord (April 1775) and Bunker Hill (June 1775) demonstrated that war had already begun and made independence from Britain appear as the only possible path.
    Historical perspectives
    • Thomas Hutchinson (1768): ‘Many of the common people have been in a frenzy, and talk’d of dying in defence of their liberties.’
    • John Adams (1765): ‘The People, even to the lowest Ranks, have become more attentive to their Liberties, more inquisitive about them, and more determined to defend them, than they were ever before known or had occasion to be.’
    Historical interpretations
    • Gordon S. Wood:
      • ‘[Colonists] were not prepared to accept [British authority] when after 1763 it tried to intrude into their lives.’
      • ‘Much of the activity of the revolutionary committees in 1774 to 1776 was devoted to breaking these older personal ties of dependency on royal authority and to establishing new attachments to “the body of the people”.’
    • Robert Middlekauff: ‘There was a powerful constitutional case against the supremacy of Parliament in the colonies; it had been stated repeatedly since 1765.’
    • Howard Zinn:
      • When discussing the economic grievances of the lower classes in Boston in the years prior to revolution, Zinn suggests that ‘the leaders of the independence movement wanted to use that mob energy against England’.
      • Zinn highlights the role of leaders such as Patrick Henry, who found ‘a language inspiring to all classes’ which was ‘stirring enough to build patriotic feeling for the resistance movement’.
    • Alan Taylor:
      • ‘The Sons of Liberty increasingly had to fill a vacuum of authority that they helped to create.’
      • ‘By declaring independence, Congress gave the conflict greater clarity and raised its stakes.’

    Sample student response Patriot groups who formed in response to British taxation and perceptions of threats to colonial rights helped to generate increasing unrest among common people in the colonies. In addition to these grassroots movements, Patriot leaders also formed extra‑legal political groups who coordinated colonial responses, displacing British authority by creating alternative governing groups. As such, while Patriot groups were pivotal in heightening colonial unrest and generating the momentum needed to break from Britain, British policy was equally significant in causing the revolution.

    After the period of salutary neglect ended, grassroots Patriot groups helped to change colonial anger about British tax revenue Acts – like the Stamp Act (1765) and Townshend Duties (1767) – into active resistance. In Boston, leaders such as Samuel Adams and John Hancock formed the Sons of Liberty to organise and lead protests against the Stamp Act, circulating pamphlets and coordinating town meetings which sometimes broke into riots and mob action. This was seen through the Boston Riots in 1765, during which Lieutenant‑Governor Hutchinson’s house was destroyed. Boycotts of British goods were promoted by the Daughters of Liberty, with non‑importation agreements organised both in 1765 and as a response to the Townshend Duties and Tea Act (1773). Continued activism saw public demonstrations and increased antagonistic attitudes towards symbols of British authority, such as the soldiers quartered in Boston. The Boston Massacre was the result of these highly inflamed social tensions in 1770. Overall, the actions of the Patriot groups in this period helped to show that collective resistance could bring about change, such as the repeal of the Stamp Act in 1765.

    But it was not just momentum that was created by these groups. As Britain implemented new laws to try to subdue the rebellious colonies, Patriot leaders built a coordinated resistance that prepared the colonies for independence. Robert Middlekauff notes that there had developed ‘a powerful constitutional case against the supremacy of Parliament in the colonies’ which had ‘been stated repeatedly since 1765’. The Committees of Correspondence (from 1772) took things one step further through improving communication, creating an intercolonial communication network that unified political responses. Provincial Congresses formed when royal governors dissolved colonial assemblies, such as with the Massachusetts Government Act in May 1774. They acted as de facto Patriot governments, organising militias and preparing colonies for armed resistance, like the Battle for Bunker Hill in June 1775. In these groups, Patriot leaders such as George Washington and John Adams went further than orchestrating mob action, shifting the activism of the early days into a more organised and coordinated political response.

    However, the changing nature of the British management of the colonies sparked much of the unrest in the pre‑revolution period. Mercantilist policies such as the Sugar (1764), Stamp (1765) and Tea (1773) Acts directly challenged colonial expectations of self‑rule and ensured economic benefit for Britain. Colonists felt discouraged by such Acts, as they saw themselves

    as British subjects entitled to ‘the full enjoyment of the fundamental rules of the British Constitution’, whereby property cannot ‘be taken from him without his consent’ (Massachusetts Circular Letter, 1768). In addition, after years of self‑rule, colonists simply ‘were not prepared to accept [British authority] when after 1763 it tried to intrude into their lives’ (Gordon Wood). On top of these constitutional arguments, the punitive nature of the Coercive Acts (1774) revealed the determination of British Parliament to quash any rebellious activity in the colonies and maintain British sovereignty by any means. The closure of Boston Harbor (Boston Port Act 1774) forced economic pressures on an already unruly population, and the removal of the elected assembly placed Massachusetts under military control. Thus, British policies and actions caused a collapse in trust, leading directly to calls for independence from Patriot leaders.

    Overall, Patriot groups were pivotal in garnering mass participation to protest against the British, heightening colonial unrest and turning community anger into coherent and organised resistance. They also ensured a coordinated and unified approach from what had been a group of separate colonies. But it was clearly the policies of the British that created the protests in the first place, and their heavy‑handed actions ensured that colonists eventually responded with the formation of both military and political groups tasked with bringing about independence from Britain.

    Question 2 (20 marks) · The French Revolution
    ESSAY20 MARKS↩ Restored
    ‘Support from sympathetic nobles and clergy was crucial in enabling the outbreak of the French Revolution in 1789 because it strengthened the political position and legitimacy of the Third Estate.’

    To what extent do you agree? Use evidence to support your response.
    0 words · aim for ~700
    HTAV 2025/2026 Guide to Responses — suggested discussion points and sample material, not the only acceptable answer.
    General advice
    • This question is primarily concerned with events that enabled the outbreak of revolution. As such, students’ responses should draw on knowledge from Area of Study 1. However, as the question does not specify a precise end date beyond ‘in 1789’, students may briefly refer to events from Area of Study 2 that occurred within 1789. Students will not be rewarded for evidence drawn from beyond 1789.
    • To achieve high marks, it is recommended that students follow this essay structure:
      • Introduction that clearly states their contention and outlines their main arguments
      • At least three body paragraphs, each clearly focused on one argument
      • A brief conclusion, restating the extent to which they agreed with the view in the essay prompt
    • The prompt contains three ideas students need to evaluate:
      • Whether or not support from sympathetic nobles and clergy strengthened the political position and legitimacy of the Third Estate
      • Whether or not this explains why such support was crucial in enabling the French Revolution
      • Whether or not support from sympathetic nobles and clergy can be considered crucial at all, or whether other factors were equally or more significant
    • Students can approach this question by:
      • agreeing fully with the view – finding several ways in which the viewpoint can be considered true
      • agreeing to some extent – supporting some aspects of the view while challenging others
      • disagreeing fully with the view – arguing that support from sympathetic nobles and clergy was not crucial and that other factors were more significant.
    • In Section B, to achieve the highest possible marks, students must effectively use historical interpretations in their response.
    Suggested discussion points
    Examples of support from sympathetic nobles and clergy
    • Some nobles and members of the clergy disseminated Enlightenment ideas both directly (e.g., What Is the Third Estate?, Society of 1789) and indirectly (e.g., involvement in salon discussions).
    • They crossed the floor of the Estates‑General.
    • They joined in the establishment of the National Assembly.
    • They showed vocal support of liberal nobles (various examples across the Study Design from individuals such as the Comte de Mirabeau, the Marquis de Lafayette, and the Duc d’Orléans).
    • They publicly renounced their privileges (e.g., Night of Patriotic Delirium).
    Evidence to support the view given in the question
    • The dissemination of Enlightenment ideas and vocal support by various nobles gave Third Estate demands elite credibility, split the privileged orders, and helped portray reform as representing the nation.
    • When parish priests and sympathetic nobles joined the Third Estate in the National Assembly, this helped to strengthen its claim to speak for France and further boosted its political legitimacy.
    • The renouncing of privileges during the Night of Patriotic Delirium signalled elite endorsement of equality and the end of privilege, reinforcing the Third Estate’s legitimacy to reform the system.
    Evidence to challenge or qualify the view given in the question
    • The Third Estate initiated key political breaks itself. It pushed voting by head, declared the National Assembly, and made the Tennis Court Oath, asserting that sovereignty came from the nation.
    • Elite support was limited and uneven. In particular, noble support was individual rather than collective.
    • Popular support sustained the momentum of the revolution. Events such as the storming of the Bastille and the Great Fear demonstrate how the masses forced themselves into politics.

    Sample student response While the Third Estate played a significant role in driving the French Revolution, support by sympathetic members of the privileged orders was crucial in enabling it. Actions by members of the clergy and nobility helped transform the Third Estate’s grievances into legitimate claims to represent France during the early stages of 1789. However, this contribution was uneven and largely confined to the beginning of the revolution, meaning it assisted rather than determined the course of events.

    The clergy were among the first key allies of the Third Estate, legitimising its claims for reform. The First Estate was internally divided between wealthy bishops and common parish priests. Simon Schama describes this as a harsh expression of the separation between rich and poor in the old regime.

    Parish priests often lived and worked in conditions similar to those of the Third Estate – for example, they earned less than 1000 livres annually. In comparison, bishops earned anywhere between 100 and 500 times more, depending on rank. As a result, both groups expressed grievances rooted in inequality, frequently expressed in the cahiers de doléances through demands for fairer taxation and representation. This shared sense of injustice helps explain why many clergy sympathised with the Third Estate’s call for joint verification in the Estates‑General, with almost half of their delegation voting in favour of it (May 1789). This intensified in June, when parish priests crossed the floor of the Estates‑General to join the Third Estate and later the National Assembly – further legitimising its claim to speak for the nation.

    In contrast, the Second Estate supported the Third Estate through individual vocal support rather than collective action. This contributed mainly to strengthening its political position. While many nobles clung to the privileges afforded to them by the old regime (notably tax exemption and access to venal offices), some liberal nobles provided highly visible support. This challenged absolutism and fractured unity among the elite. Individuals such as the Duc d’Orléans and the Comte de Mirabeau openly criticised Louis XVI and defended the authority of representative institutions. The Duc d’Orléans’s opposition during key moments of the pre‑revolutionary crisis publicly demonstrated that it was possible to question royal authority from within the elite. Mirabeau’s refusal to disperse the National Assembly following the royal session of June 1789 was particularly significant. His insistence that deputies remained ‘by the will of the nation’ reframed political authority away from the king and towards national sovereignty. Furet argues that this transfer of sovereignty was a decisive ideological shift, and noble advocates such as Mirabeau gave this idea political weight. While noble support was limited in scope, it amplified the Third Estate’s political authority at a critical moment, helping to enable the revolution.

    The support by sympathetic nobles also symbolically reinforced the Third Estate’s claim to represent the nation. This was most clearly demonstrated during the Night of Patriotic Delirium (4 August 1789), when liberal nobles publicly renounced feudal privileges including seigneurial dues and tax exemptions. While these gestures did not translate immediately into practice, they signalled a rejection of estate‑based hierarchy and offered elite endorsement of equality. Such symbolism strengthened the legitimacy of revolutionary reform by suggesting that opposition to privilege was not confined to the Third Estate. Early revolutionary documents, most notably the Declaration of the Rights of Man and Citizen (26 August 1789), reflected the principle that sovereignty lay ‘primarily in the Nation’. The fact that these ideas could be articulated and embedded in law reflected the legitimacy and political authority established in 1789, which had been strengthened by the willingness of sympathetic nobles and clergy to align themselves publicly with the Third Estate.

    However, this support should not be overstated. The Third Estate itself played the primary role in driving revolutionary momentum through political confrontation and popular action. The deadlock at the Estates‑General between May and June 1789 prompted the Third Estate’s insistence on voting by head, culminating in the declaration of the National Assembly on 17 June 1789. This was followed by the Tennis Court Oath (20 June), in which deputies vowed ‘never to separate’ until a constitution was established, directly challenging absolutist authority. These actions redefined political legitimacy by asserting that sovereignty came from the nation, not the king. This formal role was complemented by popular urban and rural action, most notably in Paris with the storming of the Bastille (14 July 1789) and in the Great Fear (late July 1789). While each is framed by slightly different contexts, they all fundamentally demonstrate the Third Estate’s willingness to force itself into the political conversation. Lefebvre interprets the Great Fear as a decisive blow against feudalism, while Soboul similarly argues that without popular mobilisation, ‘the bourgeois revolution could not have triumphed’. These interpretations suggest that while elite support helped enable early political change, revolutionary momentum rested on the actions of the Third Estate and the masses.

    Therefore, while support from sympathetic nobles and clergy was crucial, its importance was limited to particular stages of the revolution, especially early 1789 when the Third Estate sought legitimacy and protection. Clerical support and noble advocacy helped transform Third Estate demands into a national cause and protect early revolutionary institutions. As the revolution progressed and popular action became central, elite support diminished and, in some cases, turned into opposition. Although the Third Estate played a decisive role in its own liberation, the character of the revolution that emerged in 1789 was undeniably coloured by the support of sympathetic nobles and clergy.

    Assessment criteria for Section B
    • Construction of a coherent and relevant historical argument that addresses the specific demands of the essay question
    • Demonstration of historical knowledge that is accurate and appropriate for the essay question
    • Application of historical thinking concepts such as cause and consequence, continuity and change, and/or historical significance
    • Use of sources as evidence to support a historical argument, including a range of primary sources, perspectives and historical interpretations
